TSK-322.title: Blocked names and protected prefixes are refused at any depth
context: pre-commit's only name rule is `is_env_file` (`crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/scan.rs:190-203`), and nothing refuses a secret-by-nature name deep in the tree or a change under a path a project protects (https://github.com/sathyassn/codeflow/issues/174). This task adds the path gate (design foundation F5) under decisions 7 and 12:

items.text: Keys: `git.path_policy` (a level, `block` by default); `git.blocked_names` (a string, or `{pattern, except_under, reason}`); `git.protected_paths` (`{prefix, allow: [{path, reason}]}`).

Patterns: without `/`, a glob on the final component; with `/`, a component sequence at any depth; a `protected_paths` prefix is root-anchored on component boundaries; `except_under` and `allow` are root-anchored and normalized; a root entry is a whole-rule waiver that `doctor` names.

Comparison: patterns, paths and the built-in exemption list are all NFC-normalized and folded with one fixed ASCII fold; a trailing dot or space, `.`, `..`, an empty or non-UTF-8 component, or a backslash refuses; git objects only.

Links and gitlinks: a symlink is a hit when its path is a hit or its normalized target is absolute, holds `..`, or lands in a blocked name or protected prefix; a gitlink is an addition at its path; neither is followed.

Walk: the commits `base..head` introduces; a non-merge commit by its parent diff; a merge by its remerge diff, so inherited parent content is not introduced; an octopus or unreadable merge refuses; add-then-delete refuses.

Change kinds: blocked names refuse additions, renames into, content and type changes, and allow deletion with a history note; protected prefixes refuse every kind; pre-commit judges the same kinds over staged changes.

Where: pre-commit reading landed policy (refuse when unreadable; the stricter of landed and worktree when both read; the no-remote and unborn cases of `landed_policy.rs:58-72` kept); `ci` from the target's policy. Exceptions come only from the target's policy; no actor, branch, slug or body text discharges a path. Denials union; `except_under` and `allow` intersect, through a typed composition API this task adds beside `landed_policy::stricter` (`crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/landed_policy.rs`). Until 2026-10-18 TSK-320 was to add that API; with this task moved to 3.2.0 and TSK-320 in 4.1.0, this task adds it for its own keys and TSK-320 extends it.

The gate never judges its own inputs: `.codeflow/policy.json`, `.codeflow/project.toml`, `.codeflow/bootstrap.sh`, `.codeflow/bootstrap.ps1`, `.codeflow/ci-setup.sh`, `.codeflow/git-hooks/*`, `.github/workflows/codeflow-policy.yml`, `.github/workflows/codeflow-ci.yml` and every `.gitignore` are outside the four new rules whatever the policy says, compared with the same normalization and fold. Other CodeFlow or host rules may still refuse them (decision 12).
`is_env_file` and the content secret scan stay on `git.secret_scan`; `git.path_policy: off` removes only the new gate.

Shipped default names (decision 7): the `.env` family; `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`, `*.pfx`, `*.jks`, `*.keystore`; `id_rsa*`, `id_dsa*`, `id_ecdsa*`, `id_ed25519*`; `.netrc`, `.pgpass`; `*.tfstate`, `*.tfstate.*`; `kubeconfig`; the sequences `.kube/config` and `.aws/credentials`; `application_default_credentials.json`.

context: The ignore-file and size rules are TSK-323.

TSK-323.title: Ignored and oversized files are judged by the default branch's size and ignore rules
TSK-323.about: After this merges, an adopter is warned about ignored files and files larger than 1 MiB, and a new scaffold refuses files larger than 10 MiB with the routes to admit them, all judged by the default branch's policy.
context: The second step of https://github.com/sathyassn/codeflow/issues/174, on TSK-322's path gate: a file the project's own ignore rules exclude, or a file over a size limit, can still be committed. This task adds two keys, read at the policy authority, the default branch at one SHA (TSK-1077), never the working tree or a pull request's base:

items.text: `git.ignored_files` (`{level, allow: [{path, reason}]}`, default level `warn`): the authority's `.gitignore` files through a gitignore matcher; a tracked file is still tested; a `.gitignore` edit in the range admits nothing.

`git.max_file_bytes` (`{limit, except_under}`): on by default; a new or changed file larger than 1 MiB warns; in a new scaffold, a new or changed file larger than 10 MiB is refused; an updated project gets report lines only, for both thresholds, until it opts in; an explicit `limit` or `except_under` in the authority's policy replaces the default.

context: Both honour TSK-322's built-in exemption and its normalization. The matcher needs the `ignore` crate or an equivalent, a new dependency, so a tier-3 decision is recorded before any code (`Cargo.toml:36` holds `unicode-normalization`; `ignore` is not yet a dependency). Non-goal: a type rule beyond the name patterns TSK-322 already gives.

A refused file has three admission routes: (1) Git LFS, since the gate sizes the blob git holds, which for an LFS-tracked path is the pointer, so it passes with no policy change; (2) a `limit` or `except_under` change in the policy on `main` through a reviewed pull request; (3) from 4.2.0, a per-path `admitted` row in TSK-424's register. A single-file exception does not exist in 4.0.0 beyond naming the file's directory under `except_under`. Legitimate large cases (model weights, datasets and fixtures, media, vendored binaries, installers) belong in Git LFS, or in a release asset or package registry the repository references by digest.

Amended 2026-10-29 by the content policy amendment (issue #279, design revision 5, decision 8, taken by the operator that day with the admission routes stated). Until then this record said both keys were off by default and read at the base revision, with `ignored_files` at level `off`. Reasons for the change: two keys that are off protect nobody on the day they ship (decision 8 (b)), and the default branch is the only policy authority (TSK-1077, decision 5). This task stays a feature on this line by the operator's placement of 2026-10-18 and is not relabelled.

TSK-324.title: A fresh clone installs the pinned binary and wires the hooks

next.reason: task TSK-324 depends on TSK-325, whose anchored status is 'todo', not complete

context: A fresh clone carries the hook shims and policy but not the binary, git wires nothing on clone, and the shims' repair line points at the `releases/latest` installer, which can install a version newer than the project pins (https://github.com/sathyassn/codeflow/issues/170). This task ships one managed setup step under decisions 13, 14, 16 and 17:

items.text: Managed files `.codeflow/bootstrap.sh` and `.codeflow/bootstrap.ps1` at every tier, integrity paths through TSK-325.

Inputs: only `scaffold_version` and `[scaffold_sha256]` from the committed `.codeflow/project.toml`, by a strict line pattern, checked by `is_version` and `is_digest` before any URL, path or shell word; the TOML is never sourced. Origin: the `https` GitHub releases host compiled in, no environment override, `file://` refused, redirects only to `https`.

Verification: the archive must match the table's digest and the release's `sha256.sum`; a missing table, entry or match installs nothing, so a maintainer with a binary lands `codeflow update --pin <version>` first (decision 13).

Install: download and extract privately with a lock; refuse traversing, absolute, link or unexpected entries; keep the verified binary in `~/.codeflow/versions/<version>-<archive digest>/codeflow` with its own SHA-256 recorded beside it; place it in the installer directory the `releases/latest` installer uses, named in the output, when no `codeflow` is there, when the one there is older, or when it has this pin's version with a different hash. A newer one stays (`ahead of pin`); the shared binary is never downgraded by any flag (decision 16).

Under `CI`: the script exits early, before any download, install or wiring, printing "skipped: nothing installed or verified; the managed CI installer owns installation", exit 0. It runs neither `codeflow setup` nor a doctor check.

Completion outside `CI`: exactly one of `verified` (the `codeflow` on the launching `PATH` hashes to the recorded digest; exit 0), `installed` (exit 0), `ahead of pin` (exit 0), or a refusal (non-zero). After `verified`, `installed` or `ahead of pin` only, it runs `codeflow setup`, `codeflow doctor --check hooks` and `codeflow doctor --check policy-source`; after a refusal it wires nothing.

`codeflow setup`: sets `core.hooksPath` to the shim path only when unset, as `init` does; leaves a detected hook manager alone and prints its integration; records `git_hooks`; writes nothing else; arms, never disarms; no download, no `update`.

In-session selection of the hook binary is a fixed refusal (`Violation::always_blocking`, decision 17): an assignment of `CODEFLOW_HOOK_BINARY` (leading, `export`, `env`, `declare`); a git command whose process would run with a `PATH` under which `codeflow` resolves to a different file than under the launching `PATH`, judged from a leading assignment, an earlier `export`, `declare -x` or assignment-only segment, a plain `declare`, `typeset` or `readonly` of an already-exported `PATH`, and a prefix on a wrapper (`sh -c`, `bash -c`, the other shells git-guard unwraps, `env`, `xargs`, `command`) whose body expands to git, taking reassignments in order and each wrapper's and sourced file's scope; the same words in a direct script operand of `sh`, `bash`, `zsh`, `dash`, `ksh`, `ash` or `pwsh` or a file read by `source`, `.` or pwsh dot-source, tokenized one level; an unreadable or non-UTF-8 operand refuses. A `PATH` value the guard cannot resolve (an unresolved expansion) is never treated as an unchanged resolution: it refuses, or is recorded as a stated parser limit. An assignment that leaves the resolution unchanged is allowed; the binary's own export to its git children is untouched. The development route is the environment that launches the session.

`ci` compares `.codeflow/bootstrap.sh`, `.codeflow/bootstrap.ps1` and `.codeflow/git-hooks/*` with the judging binary's embedded copies, or the target's bytes when unchanged; equal to neither blocks whatever the level (decision 14).
Never: the script runs `update` or `init`; a hook or guard runs the script; a missing binary admits anything while the hooks are loaded.

context: The sample adopter repository of TSK-303 (EPC-023, 4.1.0) can serve this task's fresh-clone journey.

TSK-325.title: Edit denies cover every workflow file, the CI hook, scanners and bootstrap

next.reason: task TSK-325 depends on TSK-284, whose anchored status is 'todo', not complete

context: Several files that decide enforcement are not in the in-session edit denies (`crates/codeflow-core/src/security/actions.json:670-689`): the policy workflow, the CI setup hook (`docs/adoption.md:396`), the scanner configuration (`docs/adoption.md:397-398`), and the bootstrap scripts TSK-324 adds (adopter design section 9). This task adds exactly eight paths to `claude_edit_denies` (decision 8): `.github/workflows/codeflow-policy.yml`, `.codeflow/ci-setup.sh`, `.gitleaksignore`, `.gitleaks.toml`, `.gitleaks.json`, `osv-scanner.toml`, `.codeflow/bootstrap.sh` and `.codeflow/bootstrap.ps1`. The Codex read-only list and the presets are regenerated, and git-guard refuses the known writers to each. `.gitignore` is deliberately not added. The writer lock path and the publication directory are TSK-321's additions, not this task's. Changing these files becomes a human-only act in agent sessions; the writer boundary (what the guards can and cannot see) is stated in the docs. Non-goal: `.codeflow/manifest.json` and `.codeflow/.baseline/` (tracked once as a candidate, EPC-023 planning notes).

Widened on 2026-10-18 (EPC-022 amendment, PR 255) by the primary under the operator's rule that every security gap belongs in 3.2.0: every file under `.github/workflows/` is refused, not only the policy workflow. Today only `.github/workflows/codeflow-ci.yml` is protected (`git_guard.rs:3706`, and the `Edit(/.github/workflows/codeflow-ci.yml)` deny). Reproduced on the line at `236e9d08b` with that tree's built hooks, the payloads judged and never run: a native Write to `codeflow-policy.yml`, `release.yml` or a new `other.yml` passes edit-guard; `printf x > .github/workflows/release.yml`, `tee`, and `mv x.yml .github/workflows/new.yml` or `mv .github/workflows/release.yml /tmp/r.yml` pass git-guard and exec-guard; `python3 tool.py .github/workflows/release.yml` and `python3 -c "open('.github/workflows/release.yml','w')"` pass exec-guard, which refuses the same argument naming `codeflow-ci.yml`. So the `.github/workflows/codeflow-policy.yml` entry becomes `.github/workflows/**`, which also covers the existing `codeflow-ci.yml` entry. Git commands that check out, switch to, merge, rebase onto or pull a branch carrying workflow changes keep their current verdict: the workflow change was made and reviewed elsewhere, and a person's edit outside the session still commits. Adopter effect: agents in an adopter's session can no longer write any workflow file; workflow changes become a person's act, as they already are for `codeflow-ci.yml`.

TSK-326.title: Guards judge git operands and environment supplied as data
context: Both guards can be handed a git ref, a remote, a program or an environment assignment that comes from data they cannot read, and they allow it. The TSK-283 security review (PR 195, `target/security-review-TSK-283-03.md` in its worktree) confirmed these on the installed 3.1.0 build and on the TSK-283 head, with git-guard and exec-guard both allowing:

The guards resolve a value only when its text is in the command. A variable set from a command substitution, `read` or any other file or process data has no text to resolve, so the push, alias, transport and release decisions see an empty or unknown operand and pass. Severity: high. Branch protection and the pre-push hook still stop a push to a protected ref, so this is a missing in-session guard and not a way past the remote floor.

The remedy: a variable assigned from a command substitution, `read` or other data, and every `xargs`, `-I` or `{}` operand, is unresolved wherever it reaches a git ref, a remote operand, an environment assignment or a program position. The guard refuses, naming the rule and the sanctioned path (assign the value in the command, or run the command without data-supplied operands), before the push, alias, transport and release decisions. The same task closes a second, low gap found in the TSK-283 round 4 review (`target/security-review-TSK-283-04.md`): a bracket-arithmetic ref such as `git push origin HEAD:v$[2]` passes git-guard on 3.1.0 and on the TSK-283 head when `v2` is protected, while `$((2))` is refused. It has the same cause, an operand the guard does not resolve as the shell will, and it lives in the same ref-operand resolution, so it is one criterion here and not a task of its own (the sizing rule in `.codeflow/rules/workflow-discipline.md` "Planning" splits only for separate shippable value, a pinned contract, an operator decision, size or a risk boundary, and none applies: it is digits only and cannot spell `main`).

Non-goals: judging the content of a data file, and weakening the deterministic floor, which stays pre-push and branch protection. The policy reference must say that configuration or refs supplied as data through variables or `xargs` are not judged except by this refusal (the docs nit of the TSK-283 round 3 review).

TSK-327.title: The pre-push destination query is isolated from local configuration and transport
context: The pre-push hook asks the destination which branches and tags it holds (`ls-remote`) and uses the answer for three decisions: whether a pushed branch's tree is exempt from the tree checks, where the range base for the push set starts, and which policy authority the destination has. TSK-304 (PR 191) made the tree checks fail closed and hardened that query against rewritten destinations given on the command line, but its reviews left three inputs open. The TSK-304 record (Follow-ups, and `follow_ups` in its acceptance block) and its security review rounds 1 to 3 name them, with owner EPC-022 and revisit "before 3.2.0 ships":

items.text: An on-disk `url.<x>.insteadOf` setting in the repository, global or system configuration can redirect the hook's `ls-remote` to another repository. The answer then decides the exemption, the range base and the destination authority for a push that goes elsewhere. This predates TSK-304.

The range-base commands in `crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/push_set.rs` (`merge-base` and `rev-list --boundary`) read the commit-graph file, grafts and replace refs at TSK-304's head. TSK-287 owns this fix, and this task does not redo it. At TSK-287's reviewed commit 0cc98b23f (PR 194 now at 8bb7a22ef), its AC-1 covers forged commit-graphs and disabled subprocess commit-graph reads, and its AC-2 covers range bases (`push_set.rs:1644` and `:1659` guard both git entry points; `history.rs:308` disables commit-graph reads). TSK-327 keeps the dependency so that invariant holds once TSK-304's push set and TSK-287 are combined, and it names a range-base path only if a concrete reproduction shows one that survives both.

The destination query's ssh transport comes from the pushing environment. `batch_ssh_command` in `crates/codeflow-core/src/git/remote_query.rs` honours an inherited `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` and reads `core.sshCommand` with a plain `git` command (security review round 3, finding L2). The transport is the push's own, so the answer is no less trustworthy than the push, but the hook then depends on state the rest of the query isolates. The source rates the finding low and likely, advisory, and recommends only moving the `core.sshCommand` read to `judging_command`. This task asks for more: the query's transport selection follows a stated rule over all three selectors (below). The same function also falls back to `GIT_SSH` (`remote_query.rs:210` at TSK-304's head), and an inherited `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` masks `core.sshCommand` (`:185`), so a fix to one selector alone would leave another executable.

context: This task isolates the query: it runs with the configuration, transport and history inputs the hook chooses, and a setting it cannot isolate is reported as "cannot verify" and handled as an unchecked destination under TSK-304's rule (refuse at `block`). Hosted CI on the pushed commit stays the authority; this closes the local floor. Non-goal: changing which checks the push set holds, or reading the destination without network access.

TSK-328.title: The present close test is reliable under host load
context: `present_cli::close_ignores_other_processes_with_unreadable_command_lines` (`crates/codeflow-cli/tests/present_cli.rs`) failed once in the TSK-283 essential run 6558afd8 (`target/s2-essential-9f-present-failed.log` in the TSK-283 worktree) and passed alone and in its suite. The failure was `present close` refusing with "browser process group exists without its verifiable leader" (`crates/codeflow-present/src/browser.rs`, the macOS `process_identity` path). The test registers a stand-in browser (`sh -c 'sleep 120 & wait'` in its own process group), drops it, which kills the group and waits only for the leader, and then runs `present close`. The close treats a missing leader as gone only when the rest of the group is also gone within `LEADERLESS_GROUP_EXIT_WAIT`, two seconds. On macOS a group member that has exited but is not yet reaped still answers the signal probe (`process_group_holds_only_exited_members` can tell only on Linux), so the killed `sleep` member can outlast the wait while the host is busy.

That cause is a hypothesis: the failure was seen once, in a full gate run beside other work. The task confirms or refutes it, then makes the test reliable. The sibling test `show_after_the_browser_exited_ignores_unreadable_command_lines` builds the same fixture and gets the same check. Non-goal: lengthening a product timeout only to hide the race. If the cause is a product race (a leaderless group that is gone a moment later), the fix may be in `browser.rs`; if it is the fixture, the fix is the test.

TSK-329.title: The model evaluation gate target waits for the binary it runs
context: The `model-eval-kit` gate target can start before the binary it runs exists, and its result then depends on scheduling. In the full gate on candidate dd1188c5e (batch 2, gate run 7ba19750-cf8d-4043-a25e-a89ff2299411 under `/Users/sathya/.codeflow/gate-runs/7a134ea9c2ea8c39/`), `model-eval-kit` failed with a `FileNotFoundError` for `target/release/codeflow` in `test_closeout_inventory_matches_real_local_worktrees` (`evals/model-artifacts/test_eval_kit.py:8513`, calling `eval_kit.configure_closeout_inventory`, which runs the binary at `assets/base/agents/skills/cf-evaluate-model/scripts/eval_kit.py:3043`). `release-automation` passed in the same run. The test builds the path from `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` or `target`, plus `release/codeflow` (`test_eval_kit.py:8509`). `.codeflow/test-config.json` declares `model-eval-kit` with no `requires`, and it runs in both the essential and the full mode (`.codeflow/test-config.json:282`), so nothing orders it after a producer of that binary in either mode. It passed in batch 1 and in a targeted rerun only because a binary was already there.

No target in the gate is shown to build `target/release/codeflow`. The archived run gives `release-automation` the debug binary (`CODEFLOW_BIN` ending in `target/debug/codeflow`, from the declared `codeflow-bin` target, `.codeflow/test-config.json:114`; `scripts/test_release.py:33` and its fallback build at `:39` to `:51`), so the pass of `release-automation` proves neither that the release binary existed nor an ordering. The release-profile test targets are full-only (`read-benchmark` at `:460`, `prose-exhaustive` at `:476`), and `present-binary-delta` builds under its own `target/binary-delta-*` directory. The inventory test states no release-profile requirement. The builder chooses the producer path and records why:

items.text: use the existing `codeflow-bin` contract, which the archived manifest already supplies to `model-eval-kit` as `CODEFLOW_BIN`, add `codeflow-bin` to the target's `requires`, and have the test take its binary from `CODEFLOW_BIN` before any path under `target/`; or

if a release-profile binary is necessary, say why, and name an explicit producer target, declared in `requires`, that is available in both modes. A test that builds its own binary is not an option, because the producer must be a declared prerequisite that runs before the consumer.

context: Adding `requires: [release-automation]` is not a repair, because that target does not build the release binary.

The outcome is that `model-eval-kit` succeeds in each supported gate mode, with only its declared prerequisites, from an empty artifact directory, whatever order the scheduler picks. Non-goals: changing what the evaluation kit tests, or switching the gate to serial execution.

TSK-330.title: Hooks stay usable while a CodeFlow settings file has merge conflicts
context: When `.codeflow/project.toml` holds merge conflict markers, every CodeFlow hook refuses every command, so an adopter's agent cannot take part in resolving the conflict. Reproduced on 2026-10-16 with the installed 3.1.0 build in a scratch repository: after a merge left `tier` conflicted in `project.toml`, `codeflow hook git-guard`, `exec-guard` and `edit-guard` each exited 2 with `cannot parse project settings: invalid key` for `git status`, `git checkout --theirs .codeflow/project.toml`, `git merge --abort`, plain `ls` and an Edit of an unrelated `README.md`. After `git merge --abort`, run outside the session, the same `ls` passed. A conflicted `.codeflow/policy.json` locks the session out the same way (`cannot parse policy ... key must be a string`, reproduced the same day), so this task covers both settings files the hooks parse.

The refusal comes from `read_project_toml` (`crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/policy.rs:955`), reached through `policy_armed` and `effective_armed` (`policy.rs:866`, `:931`) on every `Policy::load_effective` call, and from the landed policy path (`hooks/landed_policy.rs:164`, `:180`) and `project_tier` (`hooks/guidance.rs:342`). Failing closed on an unreadable settings file is right in general. The defect is that a conflict the adopter is resolving leaves no sanctioned path inside the session.
The outcome is that a conflict in either settings file can be resolved or abandoned from the session, while every guard gives the verdict the ordinary effective policy gives.
Conflict recovery only replaces a local settings read that would otherwise fail. It never changes which policy is the authority:

items.text: The authority stays what `landed_policy.rs` selects: the default branch at the fetched remote, resolved to one SHA (TSK-1077, ADR-0091), with no line, task record or working copy supplying policy, and HEAD only where the no-tracking rule already uses it. Amended 2026-10-31: earlier text composed the default branch with a declared integration line by `stricter`; TSK-1077 removes that composition, so this task no longer requires it. Protected refs, root-branch selection and every level are chosen the same way, as is any enrolled baseline that TSK-320 composes later.

Where a hook reads the local file (the `policy_armed` read, `policy.rs:931`; the local comparison in `finish`, `landed_policy.rs:178` to `:180`; `project_tier`, `guidance.rs:342`), the unreadable working copy is replaced by the copy committed at `HEAD`, read as git data, for that input only, with one note naming the file. Where a read can be dropped instead (for example, `policy_armed` is ignored once a commit exists, `policy.rs:856`), the builder may drop it and record why.
Recovery starts only on unmerged index entries for the path (stages 1 to 3). Conflict marker text alone is not evidence: a file that does not parse with no unmerged entry refuses as today.
An authority that cannot be read is never replaced by defaults: the hook refuses, naming the source.

context: Hook integrity is unchanged: a Bash write to a settings file is refused as today.

Non-goals: accepting a settings file that is unreadable for any reason other than an unresolved conflict (that still refuses, naming the file), and changing what any guard refuses once the file parses.

TSK-331.title: Essential gate runs are serialized like full runs
context: `codeflow test` takes the machine gate lock only in full mode: `guard_gate` returns before the lock for any other mode (`crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/test.rs:198`), and the lock itself is `full-gate.lock` under the CodeFlow home and under the git common directory (`crates/codeflow-core/src/testing/gate_guard.rs:54`, `:215`). Essential runs from several worktrees on one machine therefore overlap, with each other and with a full gate, and their targets time each other out, the failure TSK-134 fixed for full runs. In this repository, essential runs the workspace tests, clippy and docs (15 essential targets in `.codeflow/test-config.json`).

The outcome is that on one machine an essential or full run never overlaps another essential or full run: the second run refuses at once, naming the holder, its mode and its directory. As amended on 2026-10-17, a quick run's light targets are unaffected and its heavy targets follow the same lock.
Decisions recorded here:

items.text: **One shared lock.** Essential takes the same lock files as full; there is no second lock and no per-mode policy table. The protection sought is one heavy gate at a time, and essential beside full times out just as two full runs do. Keeping the files also means a 3.1 binary running a full gate and this build running an essential one still exclude each other, and the shipped sandbox presets already allow `~/.codeflow/locks`. The file keeps the name `full-gate.lock`; the docs say it serves both modes.
**Refuse, do not queue.** The second run refuses as a second full gate does today, with the holder's mode added to the message. Waiting is not added here.

**The lock follows the heavy work, not only the mode.** `--mode essential` and `--mode full` take it for the whole run. Amended 2026-10-17 after the Codex review of PR 226 (finding F5): a quick run takes it only for its heavy targets. A target is heavy when the test config declares it heavy; in a project whose config defines no `quick` targets, where quick runs the essential targets (`crates/codeflow-core/src/testing/gate.rs:735`), every target counts as heavy unless declared light. Light quick targets run without the lock, beside any gate. This repository declares its heavy quick targets (workspace clippy at least). The pre-push gate runs quick through `run_gate_exact` (`crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/git_hook.rs:1280`) and follows the same rule; its ref, range, authority and checked-out-tree checks are unchanged.

**Waiting is bounded.** A heavy quick target that meets a held lock waits up to a bound the repository config sets, default zero, then refuses naming the holder; the run reports which light targets ran.

**Direct heavy work.** The engine cannot see a `cargo` command run directly. A sanctioned wrapper runs a direct heavy command under the same lock and cleans up its process group (provisional name `codeflow reserve -- <command>`; the builder settles the shape), and this repository's contract says heavy direct Cargo work uses it while another worktree may be gating.

context: Non-goals: an unbounded queue, and any fixed worker cap for adopters.

Amended 2026-10-17 by the gate efficiency amendment of EPC-022, from the gate speed discovery of that day (ranked change 5). The lock keeps a second heavy gate off the machine, but one gate still contends with itself: `execution.max_parallel` is 3 and counts target processes, not the workers inside them, so Cargo builds, clippy, nextest and the shell oracle (up to eight workers of its own, `crates/codeflow-cli/tests/prose_oracle.rs`) each size themselves to the whole machine. `rust-build`, `codeflow-bin` and `rust-clippy` reported Cargo lock waits in all three inspected recent essential runs. The task therefore also gives heavy targets inside one gate one worker budget and stops this repository's Cargo producers waiting on each other (AC-8 and AC-9). The budget starts as a setting of this repository (about eight workers on the 10-CPU reference host, two left for the host); an engine change to the runner is made only if configuration cannot express it, and the reason is stated. No fixed cap is added for adopters. Over-serializing also costs time, so the change is adopted only on measured elapsed time. Widened 2026-10-22 by the EPC-022 amendment of that day for issue #276: a project where several agent sessions push from separate worktrees saw two quick sets overlap and fail targets that pass alone (the quick suites run 420 to 456 s against a 600 s limit and are undeclared, so AC-2 leaves them light), and the `pgrep` check agents used before pushing is a race. The lock decision (one lock, refuse by default, bounded wait by setting) is unchanged.

TSK-332.title: A docs portal workflow lease whose owner has exited is reclaimed at once
context: The docs portal's `check`, `build`, `dev` and `preview` scripts hold one workflow lease, `.portal/workflow.lock` (`docs-portal/scripts/publication.mjs:19`, `withWorkflowLease`). The lease records only a token and two times (`publication.mjs:34`). A contender treats it as live while its heartbeat is younger than `WORKFLOW_LEASE_MAX_AGE_MS`, four hours (`publication.mjs:16`, `:50`), although the owner writes a heartbeat every 30 seconds (`publication.mjs:66` to `:73`). So a portal run that is killed (a timed-out gate target, a closed terminal, `kill -9`) leaves a lease that refuses every `check` and `build` with "portal build/check workflow already in progress" for up to four hours, and nothing checks whether its owner still runs. The same file ships to adopters as `assets/docs-portal/starter/scripts/publication.mjs`, byte-identical today.

The lease owner is the workflow, not only its coordinating process. The workflow holds the lease while it spawns the adapter, Astro and evidence children (`docs-portal/scripts/workflow.mjs:12`, `:31` to `:36`). The signal-aware lifecycle stops those children on `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM` (`docs-portal/scripts/child-lifecycle.mjs`), but `SIGKILL` of the coordinator runs no cleanup, so a child can outlive it and keep writing `dist`, generated content or caches. A dead coordinator therefore does not prove the workflow has stopped writing.

The outcome is that a lease whose whole workflow has stopped (the coordinator and every writer it started) is reclaimed at once, with a message naming the dead owner, while a live coordinator or a live writer still blocks. The lease records its owner: the coordinator's process id and host, plus whatever the builder needs against process id reuse (such as a process start time), and either the writers it starts or a mechanism that proves no writer can outlive the coordinator (for example a process group the contender can check, or children that exit with their parent). The builder chooses and records which. A contender on the same host checks the coordinator and its writers before applying the age rule. Where liveness of the coordinator or of any writer cannot be decided (another host, a lease written by an older version without an owner, a permission error on the check), the four-hour rule stays. A reused process id reads as live, which blocks; that is the safe direction.
Non-goals: the publication lease (`PUBLICATION_LEASE_MAX_AGE_MS`, `publication.mjs:15`) and changing the four-hour age for leases whose owner cannot be checked.

TSK-333.title: Version pins compare with one parser everywhere
context: TSK-309 (PR https://github.com/sathyassn/codeflow/pull/207, not yet landed) replaces the loose version parse in `crates/codeflow-core/src/scaffold/version.rs` with a strict one that returns nothing for a version that is not `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` with an optional prerelease and build, and guards init and update with it (`check_write_version`). Its review (finding N2, tracked on PR 207) found that two other paths still differ:

items.text: `is_older` now falls back to plain string order when either side does not parse, where the line's version (`version.rs:9` to `:31`) read missing or non-numeric parts as 0. A hand-edited pin such as `3.10` or `10.0` therefore compares differently after TSK-309 in the two other callers: `update --pin` refusing a lower pin (`crates/codeflow-core/src/scaffold/release_pin.rs:418`) and doctor's lowered-pin warning (`crates/codeflow-core/src/doctor/ci_pin.rs:258`). For example, `"10.0" < "9.0"` as strings.

`pin_release` (`release_pin.rs:397`) accepts any value that passes the looser `is_version` (`release_pin.rs:342`, checked at `:403`) and writes it to `scaffold_version` (`:463`). So `update --pin` can write a pin that TSK-309's guard then refuses for every later `init` and `update` as not parseable.

context: The outcome is that every comparison of versions and every writer of a pin uses the one parser TSK-309 adds, and no caller compares an unparseable version as a string: `pin_release` refuses a version the parser rejects before it fetches or writes anything; the lower-pin check and doctor's pin comparison report an unparseable pin by name instead of comparing it; the skew warning (`version.rs:38`) stays quiet or names the unparseable pin, the builder chooses which and records why. The comparison API makes the unparseable case explicit (for example a result the caller must handle) so a new caller cannot reintroduce a string order.

Non-goals: version handling in `scripts/release.py`, the installers' format check (the strict form is a subset of what they read, so they keep accepting every pin this task allows), and TSK-309's own criteria.

Scope added after the whole-unit review (2026-10-22): the `codeflow_older` shell function in the three shipped CI templates (`assets/base/ci/ci-generic.sh`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `bitbucket-pipelines.yml`) ordered pins with awk arithmetic and whole-string prerelease comparison, so it disagreed with the parser on `rc.2` against `rc.10`, on `+build` metadata and on very large numbers. It now implements the parser's precedence rules and refuses an unparseable version (exit 2), and a test runs it against `is_older` over one table. Doctor's `ci-perimeter` pin check also validates every pin it reads before any success report.

TSK-335.title: Secret-path spellings receive the same verdict
context: Issue: #180. This is related to proposal A by security boundary, but its root is the matcher, not a missing store entry. It deserves separate regression evidence.

`security/interpreter.rs:101` passes the raw word into `matches_extended_glob` at `:132`. `security/pattern.rs:19` turns `**` into `.*` but keeps the following slash. Thus `**/id_rsa*` becomes a pattern requiring a slash, and cannot match bare `id_rsa`. The relevant deny is in `security/actions.json:636`. This is a source-level explanation of the reported difference, not just the issue author's hypothesis.

The `.env` and source-name cases are a separate explicit limitation: `interpreter.rs:123` skips entire groups with carve-outs (`actions.json:580`, `:615`). Adding `./` alone would not fix those. PR 187's `interpreter.rs:105` retains the same secret-path routine and its `carveouts.is_empty()` condition.
Outcome: **A hard-denied secret path receives the same shell verdict when spelled bare, relative or absolute.**
Source inspection is from the accepted triage at `c5c6f6f671d2bf67a77113c656b3be446fb0bea1`; runtime reproductions remain implementation evidence.

TSK-336.title: Policy and release verdicts run only the default branch's code
context: Issues: #204 and #202. These share the hosted workflow trust boundary, although credential persistence and check-name reuse are separate mechanisms. One workflow-hardening unit can cover both.

`assets/base/ci/codeflow-policy.yml:57` fixes the job name to `commit standards`; `:71` checks out the PR base SHA; `:74` installs the target-pinned binary. `:219` runs CI only on PR events while `:238` runs the registry check under the same job name on other events. Current automation profiles come from the judging policy in `crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/ci.rs:1687`; the older `target_profiles` function named by the issue is not present in `ci/adopter.rs` at this revision.

The five shipped checkout steps lack `persist-credentials: false`: `codeflow-ci.yml:49`, `:197`, `:333`, `:795` and `codeflow-policy.yml:69`. Workflow permissions are read-only (`codeflow-ci.yml:36`, `codeflow-policy.yml:62`). This constrains the token's impact but does not justify handing it to later code.

Amended 2026-10-29 by the content policy amendment (issue #279, design revision 5, unit U1; decisions 1, 3, 4 and 6 taken by the operator that day). Outcome, amended: **both hosted policy jobs run only the default branch's code at one SHA; every required policy, secret-scan and release-impact check is produced only by that code; and on the default branch only by an identity the agent cannot hold, a dedicated GitHub App (Mode A), with Mode B's permission floor kept beneath it.** The reasons:

items.text: A check bound to a job name under the Actions app id (15368) can be produced by any workflow in the repository, and a skipped same-named job counts as success (design D-3, high). Six required names on `main` are pinned only to 15368 today (live ruleset 24379074, read 2026-10-29 18:43Z).

Both hosted jobs build or install, read policy and run scripts from the pull request's base (`assets/base/ci/codeflow-policy.yml:69-76`; repo `.github/workflows/codeflow-policy.yml:73-76`, `:87-90`, `:183`; `crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/ci.rs:1971-1994`), so a line, which agents update, judges every pull request into it (D-4). "Protected integration targets remain usable" is withdrawn from AC-1.

The secret scan is the pull request's own workflow (`assets/base/ci/codeflow-ci.yml:343-470`; repo `:855`), and this repository's `release impact` job builds the head (`.github/workflows/codeflow-release.yml:28-58`) (D-5, high).

context: The design in short:

items.text: Verdict jobs in the policy workflow (`pull_request_target`, the default branch's file) run for every pull request whatever its target, never reference the environment, and are named `trusted: commit standards`, `trusted: secret scan` and, in this repository, `trusted: release impact`. The head-run `secret scan` job and this repository's head-built `release impact` job are removed in the same change, and registry-only runs get their own name, so the old names have no producer.

One authority job, only for `pull_request_target` into the default branch, is the only job that references `environment: codeflow-authority`; it mints an App installation token inside the one step that creates the `authority: commit standards`, `authority: secret scan` and `authority: release impact` check runs on the head SHA. Ruleset B (TSK-1080) pins those names to the App's id. Without the App (Mode B, the floor), the final step lists check runs and statuses of the trusted names and fails closed.
Pull requests into lines get no App check; ruleset C (TSK-1080, strict) requires the `trusted:` names pinned to 15368.

Enablement order: this task reaches `main` through the line's reviewed pull request under today's rules; from that merge until the operator runs `remote protect` and retires rulesets 24379074 and 25435656, every pull request into `main` and the lines is unmergeable (fail closed, by design). The operator's Mode A steps are listed in TSK-1080.

context: Widened 2026-10-30 after the Grok whole-diff review of PR 396 (`review-PR396-grok-01.md`, high, CWE-345). Merge admission, `ci-reuse.py admit` (`scripts/ci-reuse.py:182-207`, called from this repository's `.github/workflows/codeflow-policy.yml:171-185`), accepts the newest `codeflow-ci` `pull_request` run at the head by event, head SHA, pull request number and workflow path, and by the conclusions of the jobs named `codeflow gates` and `windows`; it never checks what those jobs ran. A `pull_request` run executes the head's own `codeflow-ci.yml`, so a head that replaces it with trivially green jobs of those two names is admitted. This is on `main` today, where both names are also required directly and pinned only to the Actions app (ruleset 24379074); PR 396 did not widen it, since admission only adds refusals there. The design above still has the trusted and authority verdicts call `admit`, so it does not close this alone.

AC-14 closes it with the standard split between trusted CI definition and untrusted code under test. The gates verdict that admission reads comes from the default branch's `codeflow-ci.yml` at the authority SHA (AC-1), with the scripts and configuration that decide which tests run and how a job concludes (the set AC-13's Findings names, such as the partition and reuse scripts) read from that SHA too. The head's code, Rust and scaffold included, is the candidate those jobs build and test, as `codeflow-ci.yml:110-127` builds it today, so an ordinary product change is still admitted. The run gets a read-only token and no secret or environment, since it executes head code. A head's own copy of the workflow or of those inputs never decides admission, and neither does a line's copy: equality with an integration base is not authority. A pull request that changes the workflow or those inputs is judged by the default branch's copy and reaches `main` by the operator's merge (Mode A), as AC-11 already states for the policy workflow.

Track once, from the same review (a nit): the adopter workflow chooses essential or full on a pull request from the head's own `.codeflow/test-config.json` (`assets/base/ci/codeflow-ci.yml:175-178`), so a head can lighten its own gate. Revisit with AC-14, which reads the same head-controlled inputs.

context: Folded in by the amendment of 2026-10-18: issue #240. items.text: Scope: only a range whose head carries the task's own criteria change, whose `--into` target is an integration line the destination confirms, where that line is the `integration_target` the task's record declares both at the line's tip and at the judged head, and where the line passes the existing trusted-line binding (`epic_line_binding`, `crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/work_start.rs:883`): the epic exists in the trusted anchor records, is not cancelled or archived, and a task of that epic there names this exact line. Any other range, including one with no `--into`, keeps today's rule.

Criteria points (the proposed selection): for that task's own change, the criteria points are the line's tip and the range base. Today acceptance derives its points from the range anchor and the run bases, and an explicit `--into` adds no point of its own; plain `codeflow ci --into <line>` gives a note only because it passes no `--policy-from`. The default branch's tip passed as `--policy-from` would no longer be a criteria point for that task. Concurrent amendments among the points that remain still give no answer (R-52 unchanged there).

Kept from main: `--policy-from` stays the policy authority and `--commits-from` the commit-history authority, so main's stricter policy still judges every commit `commits_from` selects (`push_set.rs:433`), including history already on the line. A fix that passes the line tip for both flags is out of bounds.

Completion history: every point, main and the line's history included, still counts for whether the task's completion landed elsewhere (R-52's completion test, R-60, R-119, the reopen freeze, and AC-4 and AC-5's replaced-ref rule).

Where main's copy meets the line's today: when the line merges main before its landing pull request, Git merges the two copies of the record. Overlapping edits conflict and a person resolves them; edits on different lines merge without notice. The line-to-main pull request is an epic line range (`Criteria::Amendable`, `crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/ci/acceptance.rs:318`), which skips the frozen-criteria comparison (`crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/acceptance.rs:4171`), so no automatic check surfaces competing copies there; only that pull request's reviewer and the operator's merge do. AC-16 and R-52 give no automatic guarantee at that landing.

Added enforcement at the line landing (AC-9), in the scope the operator decides: a line-to-main range that merges a task record whose criteria main and the line each amended since their common version reports the two versions and the one the merge kept. TSK-352.title: Gate selection uses proven candidate evidence against the task's line
context: Source: the gate speed discovery of 2026-10-17 (Codex peer report, ranked change 1, at line head `eaf2ed04e932186cdd26dc4a7e5740cc553acee3`) and the operator's request of the same day to make the verification gates fast without losing assurance. Amended after the Codex review of PR 226 (finding F1).

Today a run with no `--since` selects every eligible target (`crates/codeflow-core/src/testing/delivery.rs`, `select`, the "no proven comparison base" branch). Of 239 retained run records, 139 gave that reason and 100 were `--only` runs, so no unrestricted run has used change-based selection. Two further gaps stop it working even with `--since`: `green_base` needs a passed, clean, complete run at the exact base revision with the exact config digest, and only an unrestricted full run is ever recorded complete (`testing/gate.rs`, the `complete` computation). So a landed merge whose tree equals the gated candidate's tree never counts, because its revision differs. The run record's `tree` field is a digest of the tracked snapshot, not a Git tree id, so it cannot be compared with `git rev-parse <base>^{tree}`. A matching tree and config digest also say nothing about the tools, platform, environment, test membership or producer outputs a check depended on.

Outcome: quick and essential `codeflow test` runs, and the pre-push quick run, select against the task's declared line by default and skip a target only when recorded evidence covers the exact check that would run now. Full mode compares only with explicit `--since`; without it every target runs for non-selective landing evidence (security F1). Every unproven case runs and names its reason.
This task owns the evidence foundation that TSK-355 (result reuse) builds on.
Decisions recorded here:

items.text: **Default base.** The merge base of `HEAD` with the declared integration target of the task being worked on, read from the task record's `integration_target` (or the branch's work metadata). It is never guessed as `main`, never the previous commit, and never a mutable branch name used as evidence identity. An explicit `--since` stays authoritative and `--all` stays available.

**Input classes.** Each target declares an input class in the test config: `content` (it reads only declared files), or `history`, `remote`, `time` or `external` (it reads Git history, a remote, the clock, a vulnerability database or another outside source). A target with no declared class is unclassified. Only a `content` target can ever be skipped; every other class, and every unclassified target, runs.

**Per-target evidence.** The run record stores, for each executed target: its mode and exact command, the Git tree id, the digests of its declared inputs before and after it ran, the identities of the tools it declares (for example the rustc, cargo, nextest, node and python versions), the platform and architecture, evidence for the environment variables it declares as relevant (below), its test membership digest where it has one, and its producers' output digests. Missing evidence of any kind means the target runs.

**Environment evidence never stores raw values.** Amended after the Codex confirmation review of PR 226 (finding F6). Equality evidence is kept apart from displayable data. Only metadata the config marks as audited non-secret (for example a platform or locale name) may be stored as a value. Every other declared environment input is stored as an opaque keyed fingerprint (a keyed hash under a key held outside the repository and the run record, so the record cannot be used to test a guessed value), never as its value. An environment dependency marked sensitive with no safe fingerprint available, or one that is undeclared or unclassified, makes the target ineligible for selection and reuse: it runs. Sensitive and fingerprint values are redacted from gate-owned output and reports. Audited non-secret and unclassified values remain unchanged in output; equality evidence never stores raw values.

**Coverage of the check.** A target is skipped only when the qualifying run executed the same command in the same mode with matching evidence, or when the config declares a coverage relation between two commands (for example that full's `rust-coverage` runs the membership of essential's `rust-workspace`) and a test proves that relation. A full run is not assumed to cover quick-only or essential-only commands.

**Qualifying run.** A passed, clean, complete full run whose recorded Git tree equals the base's tree and whose config digest is current, and in which each credited target's inputs were unchanged during its own run.

**The landing candidate.** Selection never applies to a landing candidate's gate: the primary runs it with `--all`, and a run with any skipped or reused target is never recorded complete, so the candidate always executes every target.

**Pre-push.** The pre-push quick gate uses the same selection. Its ref, range, authority, release preflight and checked-out-tree protections (`crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/push_set.rs`, and `run_push_targets` in `crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/git_hook.rs`) are unchanged and always run.

context: Non-goals: declaring this repository's target inputs and classes (TSK-353), reusing a prior target result (TSK-355), and any change to what a complete full gate runs. Product surface: adopter-facing engine (CAP-004 test gate, the test config schema) and the pre-push hook path.
