TSK-406.title: Shell expansions cannot hide a checkout from the guards
context: Sources: the security reviews of PR 246 (TSK-377) on 2026-10-18, findings SEC-377-14, SEC-377-15 and SEC-377-16, and Grok 4.7's rounds 4 and 5 of the same PR, finding R4-1 and the round 5 `git worktree move` case. TSK-377's Closeout names this task as their owner before it had an ID. All are pre-existing: the released 3.1.0 binary also allows R4-1 and SEC-377-16, judged with the commands never executed. The Codex review of PR 255 (round 1) added the `cd` case and corrected the fail-before cases below.

Reproduced on the line at `236e9d08b` with that tree's built hooks, payload cwd the main checkout and `<w>` a registered worktree under `.worktrees/`, the commands judged and never run. Each case names the guard that owns its route:

head: Route and owning guard
Allowed today (fail-before case)
Refused today (literal or preservation case)
rows: `python3 -c "import shutil; shutil.rmtree('$PWD/.worktrees/<w>')"`; the same `shutil.rmtree("$PWD/.worktrees/<w>")` in an unquoted heredoc
`python3 -c "open('$PWD/.claude/settings.json','w')"`, the same `open` in an unquoted heredoc
`rm -rf $PWD/.worktrees/<w>` with the hook process's `PWD` elsewhere; `cd docs && rm -rf $PWD/../.worktrees/<w>`

context: The refused enforcement-file forms already refuse because exec-guard judges opaque and composed text against enforcement-path tails (`crates/codeflow-core/src/security/arguments.rs:130-157`); they stay as preservation tests. The checkout-root forms have no such fallback, which is the defect. git-guard has no interpreter route: exec-guard owns every interpreter refusal, and this task does not add one to git-guard.
The defects:

items.text: **Interpreter arguments and code (SEC-377-14).** The interpreter checks in `crates/codeflow-core/src/security/outward.rs` and `security/interpreter.rs` do not resolve shell variables for checkout reach: `$PWD`, `${PWD}`, `$(pwd)`, `$HOME`, an assignment earlier on the line, and the same words inside double-quoted interpreter code or an unquoted heredoc.
**Static command substitution (Grok R4-1).** A command substitution whose output is fixed by its literal text, such as `$(printf %s '<code>')`, hides the code body from the checkout check.

**git-guard's `$PWD` (SEC-377-15).** `environment_value` (`crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/git_guard.rs:4030-4047`) reads `PWD` from the hook's own process environment. Replacing it with the payload cwd alone is not enough: after `cd docs`, the shell's `$PWD` is `<checkout>/docs`, so `cd docs && rm -rf $PWD/../.worktrees/<w>` reaches the worktree while the literal `cd docs && rm -rf ../.worktrees/<w>` already refuses.

**A worktree made earlier on the line (SEC-377-16, Grok round 5).** A path created by `git worktree add <path>` earlier in a command is not protected later in it, and `git worktree move .worktrees/<w> <outside> && rm -rf <outside>` also passes. Today `git worktree add -b t .worktrees/n && git -C .worktrees/n status` is refused by git-guard under `git.policy_authority`, because the new path does not exist when the line is judged; after this task it passes.

context: Outcome: **a path the shell would expand to a checkout root or an enforcement file gets the verdict of the literal path, an expansion the guard cannot resolve is refused where a registered checkout or enforcement file is reachable, and a checkout created or moved earlier on a line is protected for the rest of it.**

Two pieces of shell state are tracked at every command position and kept apart. The working directory starts at the payload cwd and changes only through `cd`, `pushd` and `popd`; every relative filesystem operand (a writer target, an interpreter argument, a link name or target) resolves from it. The `PWD` parameter starts equal to it and follows each successful `cd`, but it can also be assigned (`PWD=/private/tmp`), which changes what `$PWD` expands to and not where commands act. `$PWD` expands from the parameter; a relative path never resolves from an assigned `PWD`. Scope follows the shell: a brace group `{ ...; }` runs in the current shell, so its `cd` and assignments reach the commands after it; a subshell `( ... )`, a command substitution and a background job (`&`) keep their changes to themselves; a pipeline element runs in a subshell, except the last element where the shell runs it in the current shell (zsh, or Bash with `lastpipe`), and when the shell or that option is unknown the guard keeps both states. `&&`, `||`, `;` and newlines carry the state to the next command. Where the guard cannot know which state holds (a `cd` that may fail on an `||` branch, a `cd` to an unresolved word, `CDPATH`), it keeps every reachable state and judges the command against each. `$HOME` comes from the payload environment the guards already read. The directory set TSK-397 narrows after `cd` is the same working-directory state; whichever task lands second reuses the other's model.

Scope: assignments earlier on the line (plain and `export`), `$PWD`, `${PWD}`, `$(pwd)`, `` `pwd` ``, `$HOME` and `${HOME}`, and static command substitutions such as `$(printf %s '<literal>')`, in interpreter argv, in double-quoted interpreter code and in unquoted heredoc bodies (exec-guard), and in shell writer targets (git-guard). A path named by `git worktree add <path>` (with or without `-b`, `-B` or `--detach`), and both the source and the destination of `git worktree move <src> <dst>`, are treated as registered checkouts for the rest of the command.

Interface with TSK-407: this task provides the expansion resolver (assignments, static substitutions, `PWD` and `HOME` as command-position state). TSK-407 depends on this task and reuses that resolver for link names and link targets; neither task carries a second resolver.

Residual, kept by the operator's decision of 2026-10-15 (workspace `RELEASE-PLAN.md`, the TSK-302 scope decision): a path built by interpreter code at run time (adjacent literals, `+`, `chr()`, formatting, encoding) stays a stated residual; the OS sandbox and the permission preset are the backstop. Quoted heredocs (`<<'EOF'`) and single-quoted code are literal and keep their current verdict.

Non-goal: a full shell evaluator. A command substitution whose output depends on anything other than its literal text (a file read, another program's environment, a network call) is unresolved and is judged under the unresolved rule above.

Added by the second EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-18, under the operator's release rule of that day that every security gap belongs in 3.2.0 (workspace `RELEASE-PLAN.md`, 2026-10-18 operator decision).

TSK-407.title: A link created earlier on a command line is refused like an existing link
context: Source: the security review of PR 239 (TSK-373) on 2026-10-18, severity medium, shipped in both guards. A link that already exists is followed and refuses, but a link created earlier on the same command line is not seen, because the guards judge the line before it runs and the link is not on disk yet. Reproduced on the line at `236e9d08b` with that tree's built hooks, the commands judged and never run: git-guard and exec-guard both allow `ln -s .claude/settings.json s2 && python3 tool.py s2`, `ln -s .claude/settings.json s2 && cp x s2` and `ln -s .claude/settings.json s2 && printf x > s2`, while exec-guard refuses `python3 tool.py .claude/settings.json`.

Decision: the residual is refused, not accepted. A link created earlier on the same line is part of the shell grammar the guards model (operator decision of 2026-10-15 on TSK-302's scope), so it is judged like an existing link. Decided by the primary on 2026-10-18 under the operator's direction of that day to decide from evidence (workspace `RELEASE-PLAN.md`, "Settled under it the same day", item 2).

Outcome: **a writer or interpreter that names a link created, or possibly created, earlier on the same command line gets the verdict it would get if the link already existed, and a link whose target the guard cannot resolve is refused.**
Rule: the guards model the filesystem state that earlier commands on the line produce, and resolve every later word through it.

items.text: **Link-creating commands read:** `ln` (symbolic or hard, with `-s`, `-f`, `-n`, `-T` and `-t <dir>`), `link`, and `cp -s`, `cp -l`, `cp --symbolic-link` and `cp --link`.

**Names and targets:** a link's name and target are resolved through TSK-406's expansion resolver (assignments, static substitutions, `PWD` and `HOME` as command-position state), so `L=l; ln -s .worktrees/<w> "$L"` creates `l`. This task owns expanded link names and targets and their propagation to later writers and interpreters; it reuses TSK-406's resolver and carries no second one.

**Where the link lands:** a relative link name resolves from the command's working directory, never from an assigned `PWD` parameter (TSK-406 keeps the two apart): after `PWD=/private/tmp`, `ln -s .claude d` still creates `d` in the checkout. For the last operand, a real directory and a symbolic link to a directory are treated differently. A real directory receives the link inside it under the target's base name, with or without `-n` (`ln -sn ../.claude docs` creates `docs/.claude`, whose target resolves to `.claude`). A symbolic link to a directory is followed the same way without `-n` (`ln -s docs a && ln -sf ../.claude a` creates `docs/.claude`); with `-n` it is treated as a plain name, so `-f` replaces it (`ln -s docs a && ln -sfn .claude a` makes `a` point at `.claude`) and without `-f` the command fails. `-T` never treats the operand as a directory: it replaces a file or symbolic link with `-f`, and against a real directory the command fails, because a directory cannot be replaced by a link. A link command can fail after creating some of its links: with several targets each operand is linked in turn, and a later operand's failure does not remove the links already made (`ln -s ../.claude ../src docs`, with `docs/src` present, creates `docs/.claude` and then fails). So the guard keeps every possible filesystem effect of a link command, including the links of the operands that succeed when the command as a whole fails, for every later word reached through `&&`, `||`, `;`, a newline or any other separator. Only a failure known to happen before any change creates nothing (a single-target `-T` against a real directory, a destination directory that does not exist); where the guard cannot tell, it keeps all the possible states. The same holds for `ln -t <dir>`, `cp -s` and `cp -l` with several sources. `-t <dir>` places each target in `<dir>`.

**What a symbolic link points at:** its target text is kept as written and resolved when a later word consumes it, relative to the link's own parent directory, not the command's directory (`ln -s ../.claude docs/l` points at `.claude`). Resolution walks component by component through the line's links and the disk, as the existing walk does for links on disk (`crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/edit_guard.rs:490-513`). So a chain resolves through links created after the first one (`ln -s a b && ln -s .claude a`, then `b/settings.json` is `.claude/settings.json`). A hard link, `cp -l` or `link`, names the file its source resolves to when it is created.

**Verdict:** a later writer or interpreter word that resolves to an enforcement path or a checkout root refuses with the rule the target itself gets: git-guard owns shell writers (redirects, `tee`, copy and move destinations, in-place editors, `rm`), exec-guard owns interpreter arguments and code. A word whose resolution meets a cycle, more links than the OS follows, an unresolved expansion or glob in a link's name or target, or a path under a link the guard cannot read refuses as cannot-verify. A word that resolves to an ordinary path keeps its ordinary verdict, so `ln -s src/app.py app.py && python3 app.py` passes.

**Order:** "later" covers every list and pipeline separator (`&&`, `||`, `;`, `|`, `&`, newline), subshells, brace groups and command substitutions. Where a link may or may not exist (a link command on an `||` branch), every reachable state is judged. Filesystem changes made inside a subshell, brace group or command substitution persist for every later command; only the working directory and shell parameters are scoped, as TSK-406 defines.

context: The startup-file judgment already reads `ln` and `cp -s` or `cp -l` as link-creating commands (`crates/codeflow-core/src/security/startup.rs:2848-2867`, `copy_judgment`); this task reads the same commands for enforcement paths and checkout roots and carries the resulting state to the later words on the line.

The partial-failure behaviour was established by the Codex review of PR 255, round 3, with `/bin/ln` and GNU `ln` on a harmless temporary fixture (both returned 1 and left the first link in place); the hook verdicts below are judged strings, and no exploit was executed. Reproduced on the line at `236e9d08b` (Codex review of PR 255, rounds 1 and 3, and the drafter), payload cwd the main checkout, the commands judged and never run, both guards allowing each case through `cp -s` and the named owning guard allowing each partial-failure case (judged by Codex round 3; the `docs/src` condition held only in its native fixture, not in the checkout the hooks judged): `L=l; ln -s .worktrees/<w> "$L" && python3 tool.py l`; `ln -s a b && ln -s .claude a && printf x > b/settings.json`; `ln -s ../.claude docs/l && printf x > docs/l/settings.json`; `ln -s docs a && ln -sf ../.claude a && printf x > a/.claude/settings.json`; `ln -s docs a && ln -sfn .claude a && printf x > a/settings.json`; `ln -s .claude a && cp -s a b && printf x > b/settings.json`; `ln -s ../.claude ../src docs || printf x > docs/.claude/settings.json` and the same line with `;` (git-guard), and `ln -s ../.claude ../src docs || python3 tool.py docs/.claude/settings.json` (exec-guard). The ordinary controls `ln -s src/app.py app.py && python3 app.py`, `L=l; ln -s src/main.rs "$L" && python3 tool.py l`, `ln -s a b && ln -s src a && printf x > b/new.txt` and `ln -s ../src docs/l && printf x > docs/l/new.txt` pass today and must keep passing.

Non-goal: a link created by interpreter code (`os.symlink`, `fs.symlinkSync`) is runtime-built and stays the stated residual of the 2026-10-15 decision; the OS sandbox and the permission preset are the backstop. A link name or target written with a shell expansion is not that residual: it is in this task's scope.
Added by the second EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-18.

Widened on 2026-10-20 (EPC-022 amendment) by the primary under the operator's rule that every security gap belongs in 3.2.0, with finding F-HL of Grok 4.7's review of PR 260 (TSK-379) at `7156ae3ec`, severity high, confirmed (`.worktrees/tsk-379/target/review-TSK-379-grok-01.md`). A hard link shares the inode of an enforcement file, so a write to the new name rewrites the original, and the guards see only the name. `ln`, `cp -l` and `cp -al` of `.claude/settings.json` or `.git/config` to a name outside the enforcement set are allowed today by both guards, whether the link already exists or the line creates it, and a later redirect, interpreter argument or native Write of that name is allowed by git-guard, exec-guard and edit-guard. The reviewer proved it on one volume in a scratch fixture, the original restored afterwards: a link of `repo/.claude/settings.json` to a name under the temporary directory (same inode), then `printf PWNED > <name>` passed both guards and the file held `PWNED`; a link of `repo/.git/config`, then an appended `core.hooksPath` line passed both guards, and a following `git commit --allow-empty` in the scratch repository honored the planted hooks path (the hook marker file held `hooked`). A link across volumes cannot share an inode, so the class is same-volume only; an in-repo destination on the checkout's volume always is.

The widening rule: a destination that shares device and inode with an enforcement file or a checkout's git pointer is a write of that file. It is judged twice: on the creating command (`ln`, `cp -l`, `cp -al`, `link`, and `ln` without `-s`, which AC-2 already lists for the same-line case), which refuses as a write of the source it links, and on every later write to the name, in a later command on the same line or in a later tool call, which the guards resolve through the filesystem (device and inode) to the file it is, before the path rule runs. A plain `cp` makes a new inode and stays allowed. Reading device and inode is one `stat` of the operand per judged word, so the cost is bounded by the words the guards already resolve. The same identity rule covers a startup-class file as a direct operand: a name that is a hard link of `~/.zshrc` (`tee notes`, `printf x > notes`, with `notes` sharing that inode) is outside F1 of PR 264 below, which judged only the directory walk, and the enforcement-file wording above did not cover it, so it is added here as one spelled case: exec-guard, which owns the startup class, refuses the write as a write of the startup file, and the creating `ln ~/.zshrc notes` refuses as its link does today.

The same identity rule applies to a writer that walks a directory tree, added by the primary on 2026-10-20 from F1 of Grok 4.7's confirm review of PR 264 (TSK-380), round 2 at `1e1965723` (`.worktrees/tsk-380/target/review-TSK-380-grok-02.md`), severity major, confirmed live. `rg --pre tee` truncates every file it searches. The `--pre` root walk that PR 264 adds refuses a startup file name and a symbolic link that leaves the root (`startup.rs`, `reaches_below`, at that head), and git-guard refuses a root that is a path prefix of an enforcement file (`preprocessor_write_violation` at that head calling `holds_enforcement_files`, `crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/edit_guard.rs:1125` on the line), but a regular file under the root that is a second name of a protected inode passes both: `rg --pre tee needle <dir>` with `<dir>/notes` a hard link of `~/.zshrc` was allowed by both guards and the live run emptied the startup file; `rg --pre tee needle docs` with `docs/alias.json` a hard link of `.claude/settings.json` was allowed by both and emptied the settings file. A symbolic link in the same place is already refused. Requirement: in the `rg --pre` root walk (`startup.rs`, `reaches_below`, as PR 264 lands it) and in the native walk `holds_enforcement_files` (`edit_guard.rs`), a non-directory entry whose device and inode match a startup-class file or an enforcement file is treated as that file. Refusing every entry with a link count above one is the wrong test: ordinary files can be hard-linked, and the identity compare is exact. The scope is those two walks. The content a recursive copy or sync moves (`cp -R`, `rsync`, `ditto`) is TSK-408's judge, not this rule: a plain `cp` allocates a new inode and stays allowed, and no copy-source walk treats a matching inode as a write.

TSK-408.title: A recursive copy or sync is judged by the enforcement files it creates, replaces or deletes
context: Source: finding F6 of the `cf-security-reviewer` round 1 review of PR 260 (TSK-379) at `7156ae3ec`, severity high, confirmed, predating that PR and outside its diff (`.worktrees/tsk-379/target/review-TSK-379-security-01.md`). It is a 3.2.0 security gap under the operator's release rule of 2026-10-18.

git-guard's copy judge reads a copy or sync by its destination path: the `copies` check (`crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/git_guard.rs:5296-5309`) hands `copy_destinations` (`:5388-5417`) the destination, the sources as spelled and, for a copy into a directory, each source's base name inside it, and refuses when one of those words is an enforcement path. It never reads what the source tree holds, so a recursive copy whose source contains `.claude/settings.json` or a hook lands it on the checkout unjudged, and it never reads what a sync would delete under its destination. Allowed today by both hooks and by the base binary, the commands judged and never run except where the reviewer says so:

head: Spelling
Effect in the reviewer's scratch run
rows: lands `/src`'s `.claude` and `.git` content in a checkout
the same onto the current checkout
deleted the worktree's settings and its `.git` pointer
removes every file under `.claude` after copying it out

context: F5 of the same review, the `--remove-sent-files` and `--remove-source` spellings of the last two, is repaired inside PR 260 and is not this task.

Outcome: **a recursive copy or sync is refused when any file it would create, replace or delete under its destination is an enforcement file or a checkout's git pointer, and a copy or sync that touches none of them passes as it does today.**
Rule: the guard judges the content a recursive copy or sync moves, not only the destination word.

items.text: **Commands read:** `cp` with `-R`, `-r` or `-a`, `rsync` (its archive and recursive forms, any option whose name starts with `--delete` plus `--del`, `--remove-source-files` and its aliases) and `ditto`, in every launcher and separator form the guards already read for `cp`, on both hooks: git-guard's copy judge (`copies`, above) and exec-guard's (`crates/codeflow-core/src/security/startup.rs:2795-2807`, `ExecWriter::copies`), which for a directory copy judges the source and destination words and does not read the tree either, so each F6 spelling passed both hooks.

**What is judged:** for each source, every path the command would write under the destination, mapped by the command's own rules (cp's copy into an existing directory under the source's base name, rsync's and ditto's trailing-slash rules); for a deleting sync, every path under the destination that the source lacks; for a source-removing sync, every source file. A path in that set that is an enforcement file, a `.git` file or directory of a registered checkout, or a checkout root refuses with the rule that file gets, and the message names the file and the source it comes from.

**Reading the source:** the guard reads the source tree on disk at judgment time, bounded by the same walk limit the repository reader uses (`crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/repo.rs`). A source it cannot read (missing, unreadable, an unresolved expansion or glob, a remote `host:` or `rsync://` spelling) or a walk past the bound refuses as cannot-verify, naming the source, when the destination is inside a checkout or the guard cannot tell. A destination outside every checkout and enforcement set keeps its ordinary verdict without reading the source.

**Plain copies unchanged:** a non-recursive `cp` of a single file keeps the destination-path verdict it has today. A copy whose destination is outside every checkout (`cp -R .claude /scratch/backup`) stays allowed; it writes nothing the guards protect, and TSK-407's hard-link rule covers the one case where a copy shares an inode with the original.

context: Non-goal: archive extraction (`tar -x`, `unzip`, `git archive`) whose member names are inside the archive and not on disk; it keeps the destination-path check and the OS sandbox as its backstop, and the builder records it as the residual in the policy reference. Modelling what a copied script does when run later is TSK-378's and TSK-406's ground, not this task's.
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-20 under the operator's release rule of 2026-10-18 that every security gap belongs in 3.2.0.

TSK-411.title: A pre-push gate block names the target that failed and how
context: Issue #250. On 2026-10-18 an adopter's pre-push gate (CodeFlow 3.1.1, source `48104f48b`) blocked a push with `push set failed for: [empty]` after the push set took 578.5 s against its 60 s budget on a machine with load averages of 20 to 33. The person pushing could not tell what to fix; a retry at lower load passed, and a later block on another branch named its target after a 600 s timeout. The block message is built in `crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/git_hook.rs:1520-1545`: when the gate outcome is `Completed` with `passed` false, the failed list is every result whose `passed()` is false, so a run that ends unpassed with no result marked failed (a target that timed out or was killed without a recorded result, or an internal gate error) prints an empty list. The cause is not confirmed; this task finds it by reproduction.

Outcome: **a `git.test_gate_on_push` block always names the target that failed and how it failed (non-zero exit, timeout, killed, or an internal error of the gate itself), and when no target failed the message names the gate condition that caused the block.**
Non-goals: the push-set time budget and target serialization, which TSK-331 owns; the gate target set of any project.
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 under the operator's release rule of 2026-10-18 (a defect that blocks work belongs in 3.2.0).

TSK-412.title: The commit-time secret scan can run the pinned gitleaks rules
TSK-412.about: After this merges, a project that sets `git.secret_scan_engine: gitleaks` can have the pinned gitleaks rules refuse a staged match at commit time, and every project has the merges Git concludes itself scanned for secrets.
context: Issue #251. The pre-commit hook scans the added lines of the staged diff with a fixed set of high-signal credential shapes (`crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/git_hook.rs:110-152` calls `scan_staged`, which runs `crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/scan.rs` `scan_line`). The managed CI secret scan runs gitleaks 8.30.1 with its default rules, which include the entropy-based `generic-api-key`. A match that only the CI rule sees is found after the commit exists and other work is built on it; the adopter's only fixes are a history rewrite or a permanent `.gitleaksignore` fingerprint, each needing a person's reviewed commit. In the reporting monorepo, 7 of 23 exemptions are one spec line that passes the hook on every edit, and a file's SHA-256 recorded under its path name cost two permanent exemptions. The adopter measured `gitleaks git --staged` at 0.03 s for an empty stage and 0.06 s for a merge commit's range, so a staged scan fits the pre-commit budget.

Outcome: **a project can opt in to running the pinned gitleaks binary on the staged content at commit time, with the same rules and ignore files the managed CI scan reads, so a match is caught while it can still be reworded; the built-in patterns stay the floor, and at `block` a missing or mismatched binary fails closed.**
Decisions recorded here:

items.text: **Opt-in, not default.** A new policy key (provisional name `git.secret_scan_engine`, values `builtin` and `gitleaks`, default `builtin`), placed by TSK-280's placement rule and read by the hook (TSK-363 refuses a key with no reader). The built-in scan runs in both settings; `gitleaks` adds the binary's verdict.

**Same pins as CI.** The hook runs the gitleaks version the managed workflow pins (`assets/base/ci/codeflow-ci.yml`) and checks its checksum; at `block`, a binary that is missing, unpinned or mismatched refuses the commit and names `codeflow doctor` and the install route. At `warn` it warns once and runs the built-in scan.

**Ignore files.** The working tree's `.gitleaksignore` and `.gitleaks.toml` are read, as the only copies available before a commit exists; a commit cannot weaken CI, which reads them from the trusted base. The pull request records what a staged fingerprint looks like (the issue's open question) and documents that an existing commit-bound fingerprint never covers a staged finding, so a known false-positive file is allowlisted by path in `.gitleaks.toml`.

**The scanner makes no network request.** The hook never downloads the binary, and the scan and its gitleaks runner never fetch (a partial clone's missing object is a failed scan); `codeflow doctor` reports where it looked and the pinned version. The hook's policy-authority step may ask the configured remote once, as AC-5 (amended) states.

context: Non-goals: a local run of the full managed scan over a range (TSK-430 in EPC-024), the dependency audit, and making gitleaks the default.
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 under the operator's release rule of 2026-10-18 (a defect that forces an adopter workaround belongs in 3.2.0).

Widened 2026-10-26 for issue #296 (CodeFlow 3.1.1; unchanged at this line's `0f08dd7f8`). The staged secret scan never runs for an automatic merge commit: Git runs `pre-merge-commit` on that path and not `pre-commit`, and `pre_merge_commit` (`crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/git_hook.rs`) checks protected branches and the root checkout only, so a merge driver that writes a key neither parent holds commits it. Git writes `MERGE_HEAD` after `pre-merge-commit` runs (git v2.54.0, `builtin/merge.c:930` and `:963`), so the scan runs in `commit-msg`, which Git calls with `MERGE_MSG` for an automatic merge and with `COMMIT_EDITMSG` for plain and hand-concluded commits that already ran `pre-commit`. The built-in floor and, when chosen, the gitleaks engine both run there. This is a security gap in the default, so it rides with this task's scan work in 4.0.0 rather than waiting for the opt-in engine's users.

TSK-413.title: An inline interpreter program's git calls are read by the language's grammar
context: Issue #253. exec-guard reads the source text of an inline `python3 -c '...'` program as if it were shell git arguments. In `subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(source), "status"])` the guard takes the literal `str` as the `-C` repository path, fails to discover a repository at `<cwd>/str`, and refuses the whole command under `git.policy_authority` with the remedy "restore the command repository and its readable policy authority", which names no route that fits. The `-C` value is a Python expression evaluated at run time to a throwaway clone path. The adopter's workaround is to move the snippet into a file and run `python3 -I -B <file>`, which the guard does not read at all, so the current parse is both wrong in its explanation and easy to step around. Seen 2026-10-18 on CodeFlow 3.1.1 (`48104f48b`) in a Codex builder seat. The reader is the interpreter judge TSK-302 added (`crates/codeflow-core/src/security/interpreter.rs`); TSK-378 widens it to more interpreters and TSK-406 gives it the shell-expansion resolver.

Outcome: **a git call inside an inline interpreter program is read by that language's grammar: a string literal operand gets the literal's verdict, any other expression is unresolved and is refused only where a checkout or enforcement file is reachable, and the refusal names the expression and the sanctioned route (a literal path, or a reviewed script file). The issue's command from a checkout is therefore still refused, with the right explanation; the guard never evaluates interpreter code to decide.**

Rule: a `-C`, `--git-dir`, `--work-tree` or path operand of a git call in interpreter code is judged as a literal only when the language's grammar makes it one (a plain string literal, or a concatenation of literals); a name, call, f-string with a placeholder, or other expression is an unresolved word, judged by the same rule TSK-406 gives an unresolved shell expansion: refused where a checkout or enforcement file is reachable from the working directory, with the expression quoted in the message, and allowed otherwise. The refusal names `git.policy_authority` only when a literal path names a repository the guard cannot read.
Non-goals: reading a script file the interpreter is given (a stated residual of TSK-302, unchanged here); executing or evaluating interpreter code.
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 under the operator's release rule of 2026-10-18 (a defect that blocks work belongs in 3.2.0).

TSK-414.title: A cancelled standalone task record lands through a planning pull request
context: Issue #257. A standalone task's record was committed only on its own task branch, which also held a commit the project did not want on `main`. The task was cancelled before anything landed, and the project wanted only the cancelled record on `main` so the decision stays in the record history. A fresh `plan/` branch with one commit adding the record at `status: cancelled` was refused both ways by `codeflow ci` 3.1.1: with `Task: TSK-366`, `work.stable_planning_anchor` asked to land the record on the task branch and run `work start`, which would make a second claim for a task being cancelled; without a `Task:` line, `work.classification` asked for one, and `Task: EPC-NNN` does not apply to a task with no epic. The cancel commit stays on a local branch and the decision is recorded elsewhere.
Outcome: **a planning pull request can land a standalone task record whose status is `cancelled` and that is not present at the merge-base, with no start claim, and the docs name that route.**
Decisions recorded here:

items.text: The class is the existing planning amendment on a `plan/` branch: a record-only range that adds a standalone task record already at `cancelled` (its Closeout carrying `- cancelled:` and `- scope:`), with `Task: TSK-NNN` naming that task. `codeflow ci` accepts it without a start claim, because a cancelled task never starts, and prints the note it prints for a planning amendment with no epic.
The record must be a valid cancellation: a status other than `cancelled`, a missing reason or scope, or any path outside `project-management/` in the range keeps today's refusal.
A task record that is present at the merge-base at another status is not this route; it changes status in its own task PR or through `codeflow task status` as today.

context: Non-goals: landing the cancelled task's product commits; a route for a cancelled epic (TSK-418 covers wording edits to a cancelled epic's records).
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 under the operator's decisions of 2026-10-18 and 2026-10-22 (a defect that blocks work, and a project-management change, belong in 3.2.0).

TSK-415.title: The sed judge reads quoted delimiters and judges only sed's own writes
context: Issue #258, two cases on CodeFlow 3.1.1 (`48104f48b`), which already holds TSK-290's sed reader (`crates/codeflow-core/src/security/sed_script.rs`):

items.text: `sed -i '' 's#b#c#' "$TMPDIR/sedprobe.md"` is refused under `git.hook_integrity` as editing "repository enforcement files", while the same edit with `/` as the delimiter passes. The scratch file is outside any repository. The likely cause, not confirmed in source, is that `#` inside the quoted expression is read as a comment start, leaving the `sed -i` target unresolved and the rule failing closed.

`sed -n "/## Closeout/,$ p" <record>; rg -n "..." DOC-INDEX.md; rg -n "mode|quick" .codeflow/project.toml`, a read-only line, is refused with "`sed` takes a word the shell fills in, and the command line names the enforcement path `.codeflow/project.toml`" (`crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/git_guard.rs:4462`). The `$` is a sed address followed by a space, which the shell does not expand, and the enforcement path is an operand of a separate `rg` read. The check combines "some sed word is unresolved" with "an enforcement path appears anywhere on the line".

context: Outcome: **git-guard refuses `sed` under `git.hook_integrity` only when a path sed itself could write (an `-i` target, or a `w` or `W` command or flag) resolves to a hook, policy or settings path; a quoted `#` or a `$` that the shell does not expand is part of the argument, and a path named by another command on the line never counts against sed.**
Rules:

items.text: The shell word reader keeps a `#` that is inside quotes, or not at the start of a word, as text; a `$` followed by a space, a quote or the end of the word is text, not an expansion.

The unresolved-sed check judges only the words sed could write: the `-i` operands and the targets of `w`, `W` and the `s///w` flag, resolved by TSK-290's reader. A word the shell fills in among those stays refused where an enforcement file is reachable (TSK-406's rule). Another command's operands on the same line are judged by that command's judge alone.
The second case's `sed -n` with no `-i` and no `w` is a read and passes.

context: Non-goals: `sed` forms TSK-290 marks unproven (they stay refused), and the shell segmenter defects TSK-417 owns (newlines and braces inside quotes, variable `tee` paths).
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 under the operator's release rule of 2026-10-18 (a defect that blocks work belongs in 3.2.0).

Widened 2026-10-26 for the comment of 2026-10-26 on issue #342, the same delimiter family as #258. `cd <worktree> && sed -i '' 's|...|...|' tests/test_person_apply.py && ...`, a `|`-delimited program holding `(`, `"`, `\\r\\n`, `[ ]` and a ` # ` comment in the replacement Python text, is refused under `git.hook_integrity` although its only target is an ordinary test file. Rechecked on 2026-10-26 with the line's binary at `0f08dd7f8`: still refused, now as "`sed -i` edits the integrity path `cannot inspect every glob path: more than 4096 entries`" (3.1.0 named "repository enforcement files"). Narrowed on the same binary: `sed -i '' 's|(a)|x|' tests/x.py` and `sed -i '' 's|a # c|b|' tests/x.py` are refused with or without the `cd`, while `s/a # c/b/`, `s|a|b|`, `s|"a"|x|` and `s|a\[200\]|b|` pass. So a `|`-delimited program loses its target when it holds `(` or ` # `, and the leftover text is read as a path glob. AC-7 owns it.

TSK-416.title: Readiness and completion checks judge a line by the reference they report
context: Issue #262 and the 2026-10-22 comment on issue #278, the same cause in two commands. `codeflow work claim` reports readiness "on origin/<line>" (`crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/readiness.rs:1236`) but checks a dependency's research pin against `target_reference(repo, &line)` with the dependency's bare `integration_target`, and `target_reference_names` (`crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/work_start.rs:3039-3058`) tries `refs/heads/<target>` before `refs/remotes/origin/<target>`, so a stale local branch of the line decides readiness and refuses a pin that is on origin's tip. `codeflow task status <id> complete` judges a waiver's planning commit "on the target" the same way: with local `main` stale at a commit before the planning pull request merged, completion refused "waiver names <planning sha>, which is not on the target" although `origin/main` held it. In both cases the agent cannot repair the local branch: `git fetch origin <line>:<line>` is refused by git-guard as a policy-authority change, and fast-forwarding a protected local `main` is refused by `git.merge_to_protected`, so a person has to update the checkout. TSK-398 fixed the same local-first lookup for `codeflow ci` and pre-push anchors only (`cmd/ci.rs`).

Outcome: **every readiness and completion check that reports a reference judges against that reference: a bare target resolves to the remote-tracking ref when the remote has it, a local branch of the same name never decides, and when only a local branch exists the message says which reference was read.**

Rule: `target_reference_names` for a bare name tries `refs/remotes/origin/<target>` first and `refs/heads/<target>` only when the remote-tracking ref is absent, and every caller that reports a reference prints the one it resolved. Callers found by a search of `target_reference` and `target_reference_names` are each covered by a test. The fetch `work claim` performs stays; it updates the remote-tracking ref the check now reads.
Non-goals: moving a local branch for the user; the chain semantics TSK-341 decides; the reopened-task waiver rule TSK-340 now carries (the body of #278).
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 under the operator's release rule of 2026-10-18 (a defect that blocks work belongs in 3.2.0).

TSK-417.title: The shell reader keeps a quoted argument whole across newlines and braces
context: Issue #273 and its comment, on CodeFlow 3.1.1 (`48104f48b`) with the Claude Code Bash tool. git-guard refuses `L=/private/tmp/scratch; echo x | tee $L/probe5.log; python3 -I -c "\nprint(1)\n"` under `git.hook_integrity`, naming the later quoted Python text as part of the `tee` target ("targets the integrity path `the registered worktree <worktree>/ (through `print(1)`)`"). The same line with a literal tee path, `tee $L/x.log` alone, or a quoted string with no newline each pass. With braces in the quoted text the refusal shows the text brace-expanded, or says "a brace expansion too large to read" (`crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/git_guard.rs:2091`). The reader appears to split the command into lines, or brace-expand it, before it accounts for quoting, so a later quoted argument attaches to the unresolved variable path. The comment adds a message defect: a list that combines a `sed -i` on a variable path with `grep -c -E '^[0-9a-f]{64} l1' $R` is refused (expected, for the `sed -i`), but the message names the quoted regex quantifier `{64}` as an enforcement path and claims a directory read of more than 4096 entries.

Outcome: **inside quotes, a newline and a brace are part of one argument: they never end a command, change another command's target or expand; a `tee` to a path assigned earlier on the line resolves as it does when no multi-line string follows; and a refusal names the operand that caused it, never a quoted pattern from another command.**
Rules:

items.text: The segmenter reads quoting before it splits on newlines or expands braces: a newline or `{...}` inside single or double quotes is text. An unquoted newline ends a command as today.
Brace expansion applies to unquoted words only, and a quoted word whose text contains a brace is never read as a path glob or counted against the directory-entry limit.

A refusal under `git.hook_integrity` names the writing command and the operand the judgment rests on (here `sed -i $R`), with the unresolved-word reason TSK-406 states; other commands' quoted arguments on the line do not appear in it.

context: Non-goals: the `sed` delimiter and address cases (TSK-415); making an unresolved `sed -i` target pass (it stays refused where an enforcement file is reachable).
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 under the operator's release rule of 2026-10-18 (a defect that blocks work belongs in 3.2.0).

Widened 2026-10-26 for issue #342 (CodeFlow 3.1.1). git-guard refused a read-only `cd <worktree> && grep -c -e ... -e "externally_modified\") is True:" ... -e "ord(c) > 127" ... /dev/null` under `git.hook_integrity`, saying "redirect would overwrite the integrity path `repository enforcement files`". The only `>` is inside a double-quoted pattern, after an escaped `\"` in an earlier pattern. The issue's exact line is refused by the installed 3.1.0 binary in this repository and allowed by the line's binary at `0f08dd7f8`, where TSK-380 (search patterns are never write targets) and TSK-406 have landed. AC-7 pins the line as a regression test and adds the message rule the issue asks for: a line whose quoting the reader cannot settle is refused as unparseable, never as a named redirect. The issue's comment of 2026-10-26 (a `|`-delimited `sed -i` program) still fails at `0f08dd7f8` and is the sed reader's case, TSK-415 AC-7.

TSK-418.title: A records-only editorial change lands wording changes to many closed records
context: Issue #277. A full-tier project adopted a rule that tracked content must not name internal sessions or local paths, and must rewrite that wording across closed task and epic records while keeping every criterion id, tag, status, criterion outcome and reviewed commit. `codeflow ci` 3.1.1 refuses the edit in every pull request shape: a records-only PR naming the cleanup task (37 `work.acceptance_binding`, 24 `work.criteria_frozen`, 7 `work.records`), a `plan/` branch naming the open epics (binding, amendment and records refusals remain), one PR per completed standalone task under ADR-0080 (criteria text only, 64 PRs), and a cancelled epic, which `Task:` cannot name. The issue cites each rule's source lines at `48104f48b` and shows that the binding refusal depends on unrelated history after the landing, not on the edit. ADR-0084 on this line (TSK-278) covers one task record per PR and only its criteria and acceptance blocks, with the `review` field frozen. The project leaves closed records unchanged and registers the workaround.

Outcome: **one reviewed pull request can change only the wording of any number of closed task and epic records, across epics, standalone tasks and cancelled epics, while `codeflow ci` proves that every status, criterion id, tag, criterion outcome, reviewed commit, waiver commit and superseded-block count is unchanged and prints a per-record wording delta for the reviewer; such a record is not rebound, not read as reopened and not judged as a criteria change.**
Decisions recorded here, from the issue's suggested fix:

items.text: **Class.** A planning-records-only range on a `plan/` branch whose body declares the class with one `Records: editorial` line beside `Task: TSK-NNN`, the cleanup task, so the `Task:` line keeps one meaning. The cleanup task is an ordinary task (standalone or in an epic) whose own record may be in the range.

**What CI proves per changed record,** against the merge-base copy: same path, kind and status; frontmatter identical except the annotation ADR-0084 defines; same criteria ids, order and tags; same number of active and superseded acceptance blocks; in each block the same `reviewed`, every criterion outcome, every waiver sha, the journey outcome and the verdict. Prose sections, criteria text, block evidence and notes text, a superseded block's `reason` and `- reopened:` lines may change. A `review` field may change only when the pull request records the original as ADR-0084's digest does.

**Exemptions.** A record that passes these checks is not rebound, not read as reopened and not judged under `work.criteria_frozen`; each prints a wording delta as a note. A record that fails any check gets today's refusal, naming the field that changed.
**Remedy text.** The waiver clause leaves the binding remedy unless the refused block holds a `waived` result, and a wording edit is pointed at this class.
The decision extends ADR-0084 and is recorded as a new ADR drafted in this task's PR (Tier-3: a CI class that exempts closed records from three checks).

context: Non-goals: changing any result or outcome through this class; the single-record redaction of ADR-0084 (unchanged); cancelling or reopening a task.
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 under the operator's decisions of 2026-10-18 and 2026-10-22 (an adopter workaround, and a project-management change, belong in 3.2.0).

TSK-419.title: Epics are sized to one value line and built one at a time per stream
context: Issue #280, items 1 and 4 and the comment of 2026-10-22. A full-tier project on 3.1.1 runs 17 integration lines; several epics hold 22 to 69 tasks, and after three weeks almost no product work has reached `main`, because an epic finishes only when all of its tasks finish and each work stream held several open epics at once. `cf-method` "Planning an epic" warrants an epic by the standalone test and names no size; `cf-plan` step 5 partitions tasks by outcome and dependency. Nothing says how small an epic should be, when to open the pull request to `main`, or how many epics a stream builds at once.

Outcome: **the managed guidance says an epic is the smallest set of tasks that gives a reviewer something usable on `main`, stated as one value line ("after this merges, X can do Y"); an epic that will not fit that line is planned as two or more epics with their merge order; the pull request to `main` opens when a usable set of finished tasks is ready, with unfinished user-facing work switched off; and a work stream builds one epic at a time to completion.**
Rules the guidance states, each in plain words with an example:

items.text: **The value line.** `cf-plan` and the epic template ask for one value line in the epic's `## Outcome` section (TSK-435); `cf-method` "Planning an epic" adds it to the clarity checklist. Size numbers, where given, are an orientation range, never a cap ("Only the operator adds process").
**Split, with merge order.** A brief whose outcome needs more than one value line becomes two or more epics; the plan names which merges first and the edge between them.

**Early pull request to `main`.** Open it when a usable set of finished tasks is ready, not only when the epic is done; unfinished user-facing work stays off on `main` behind a flag, a disabled default or an unwired entry point, named in the PR, so a partial merge never shows half-built work. The epic's remaining tasks continue on the line. The precondition is TSK-433: until it lands, `codeflow ci` judges a line's own reopened and amended completions as foreign in a pull request into `main` (18 blocking findings on the 3.2.0 line head `29a217556`), so the guidance names TSK-433's class and this task is dispatched after it lands.

**One epic at a time per stream.** A stream builds one epic to completion (all tasks landed, closed, PR to `main`); the next epic's planning and reviews may run alongside, and the next build starts only while the current epic waits on something outside the stream. The managed map's "shape a request" and "land a batch" rows carry the rule.

context: Non-goals: a cap on epic size; a status view of streams (TSK-420 shows line drift; the per-stream view is TSK-311's in 4.1.0); changing how epics close.
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 under the operator's decision of that day (project-management changes go in 3.2.0). This amendment applies the rule to EPC-024.

TSK-420.title: orient reports each integration line's drift from main
context: Issue #280, item 2. In the reporting project, integration lines sit 12 to 1,201 commits behind `main`; a change on `main` stays missing on every line until someone syncs each one by hand, and nothing shows which lines have drifted. `codeflow orient` prints the session digest (`crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/orient.rs`, `crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/orient.rs`) with branch, worktree and work counts and no line view; the program report that would show every fetched line (#166, TSK-311) is 4.1.0 work.

Outcome: **`codeflow orient` and the SessionStart digest show, for each integration line the remote advertises, how many commits it is behind the protected target, when the target was last merged into it, and the age of its oldest unlanded task, and flag a line that has gone longer than a project-set interval without a sync.**
Rules:

items.text: The lines are the remote-tracking `integration/*` refs as last fetched, because `orient` is a read command and never fetches (SPC-013 R-103); with no remote or no fetched integration refs, the local lines, marked as local.

"Behind" is `git rev-list --count <line>..<target>`. The line's own commits are its first-parent chain down to, and excluding, the merge base with the target; commits at or below the merge base are inherited and never count as the line's events. A sync event is an own merge commit whose other parent is on the target; "last sync" is the newest such event by its commit date (the date the merge was made, not the merged tip's age). The line's creation is reported only from real evidence of the ref's creation (the remote's branch creation record where the provider gives one, or the local reflog entry that created the ref); without it, creation is `unknown`. The oldest own commit may be shown, labelled `oldest divergent commit`, as the historical fact it is, and never stands for creation: a line named today over month-old divergent history has an old divergent commit and an unknown creation. A line with no own commit shows `fresh, no own commits`. A line whose creation is unknown and that has no sync event gets no time-based flag. A timestamp alone establishes neither a ref's creation nor a sync event; the commit date is read only for a sync merge identified independently by its parents. "Oldest unlanded task" is the earliest `created` among the line's tasks whose records on the line are not terminal.
The interval is a policy key (provisional `git.line_sync_interval`, placed by TSK-280's rule, read by `orient`, default off) ; past it the line is flagged with the sync route TSK-421 names.
The facts are exposed through one reader the sync route (TSK-421) and the program report (TSK-311) reuse; the view stays read-only.
Streams are the coordination ledger's `WS-NNN` (EPC-025, TSK-439); this view does not read the ledger and lists epics only.

context: Non-goals: syncing or closing a line (TSK-421); the program report's per-record view (TSK-311, which reuses this reader for its line rows).
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 under the operator's decision of that day (project-management changes go in 3.2.0).

TSK-421.title: A line is synced from main and closed by one checked route each
context: Issue #280, items 3 and 5. Syncing a line from `main` is a hand-run merge today (cf-method "Managing a body of work", drift control); each sync trips record checks that judge `main`'s completed tasks again (#176, #181, #197, #217, #218, #240, owned by TSK-306, TSK-339 and TSK-340), and a sync that carries a `.github/workflows/` change needs a person to push it, because the guards refuse agent writes there (TSK-325). Nothing closes a line: a dormant or empty line keeps collecting drift.

Outcome: **one command merges the protected target into a line, runs the line's pre-push gate, and reports which merged paths a person must push, and is safe to run whenever the target changes; and one command closes a line after checking that nothing on it is unlanded, recording the closure.**
Rules:

items.text: **Sync** (provisional `codeflow line sync <line>`): fetches, merges `origin/<target>` into the line's checkout in a linked worktree with a no-fast-forward merge, refuses on a conflict naming the files, runs the quick gate through the same path the pre-push hook uses, and reports the merged paths under `.github/workflows/` and other person-pushed paths with the exact push a person runs. With no such paths it pushes the line as a durability push. A sync that lands no new commits is a no-op that says so. A clean sync produces a range `codeflow ci` and the pre-push hook accept without a waiver, which is what TSK-339 and TSK-340 deliver; this task adds the fixture that proves it on the sync route and returns any remaining re-judge to the plan as a finding. The epic or checkpoint pull request the synced line then opens into `main` is judged as TSK-433 states.

**Close** (provisional `codeflow line close <line>`): refuses while any task whose `integration_target` is the line is not terminal, any pushed task branch targets the line with a tip not on it, or the line holds commits not on the target; otherwise writes the closure (date, final tip, the epic's PR to `main` where one exists) into the epic record's planning notes through a planning commit on the target, and lists the branch deletion TSK-402's cleanup rule then allows. It never deletes the branch itself.
Both are agent-runnable under the guards: they use the sanctioned fetch, merge and push forms and never touch a protected branch.

context: Non-goals: deleting branches (TSK-402's cleanup rule); carrying one task's landed change to another line (TSK-402); the drift view (TSK-420).
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 under the operator's decision of that day (project-management changes go in 3.2.0).

TSK-433.title: The epic line's pull request into main judges the line's own completions as its own
context: Found by the primary on 2026-10-22 while rehearsing the 3.2.0 release pull request. `codeflow ci --base origin/main --head 29a217556 --branch integration/EPC-022-the-3-2-0-milestone-fixes --into main`, run with the binary built at the line's tree, gives 18 blocking findings, all `work.acceptance_binding`, two for each of nine tasks that were reopened and amended on the line (TSK-275, TSK-276, TSK-278, TSK-280, TSK-304, TSK-305, TSK-306, TSK-307 and TSK-352):

items.text: "`refs/remotes/origin/integration/EPC-022-the-3-2-0-milestone-fixes` (commit 29a217556) records a completion of this task, but it is not the target this run is judged against, so its criteria stay as they were" (`crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/landing.rs:129`);

"a reopened task keeps its criteria as the anchored target has them; change them in the epic's batched amendment, a planning pull request on the target" (`crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/acceptance.rs:2795`, `REOPENED_CRITERIA`).

context: When the epic line itself is the head of a pull request into `main`, the anchored target is `main`, so the line's own landed completions and the planning amendments that changed those tasks' criteria on the line are judged as foreign: the line is the home that TSK-339 says a completion is judged at, but here it is also the head. Every epic pull request to `main`, and every early checkpoint pull request (issue #280 item 4, TSK-419), fails the same way, so the release pull request itself is blocked. No open task owns this direction: TSK-339 judges a completion imported into a receiving line at its proven home, TSK-306 settles competing record versions at unordered judged points, TSK-340 settles the reopened completion sequence, and TSK-308 counts adopted direct commits; none of their criteria names the line-into-target pull request.

Outcome: **when a pull request's head is an integration line and its target is the protected branch, `codeflow ci` judges each task whose `integration_target` is that line against the line's own history: a completion landed on the line is bound at its line landing, criteria amended by a planning amendment on the line are the task's criteria, and a reopen and re-completion on the line is one valid sequence; and `codeflow ci` for the EPC-022 line's pull request into `main` is clean on the line head.**
Rules:

items.text: The pull request class is the epic PR (`Task: EPC-NNN`, head an `integration/` line, target the protected branch). For it, the anchored target for a task whose `integration_target` is the line is the line head, with `main` as the base of the range; a task whose target is `main` keeps today's judgment.

The line's authority is proven the way TSK-339 proves a home: the completion's landing merge on the line, the reviewed commit on the line, and the planning amendments on the line, each through the guarded history reader. A task whose line history cannot be read, or whose record on the line differs from the record at the head, stays refused.
A checkpoint pull request from the line to `main` before the epic closes (TSK-419) is the same class and gets the same judgment.

An epic line that joined the judged line, whose tip the range head contains and which passes the epic-line proof itself, is judged the same way for the tasks that declare it (amended 2026-10-28: route A joined the EPC-025 line into this line through TSK-1000). A joined line that fails the proof keeps today's refusal.

context: Non-goals: changing how a task pull request into the line is judged; waiving any task's binding; closing the epic.

Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 under the operator's release rule of 2026-10-18 (a defect that blocks work belongs in 3.2.0). It must land before the epic's pull request to `main` is opened.

Widened 2026-10-26 for issues #320 and #341, both from one adopter's `codeflow ci --into main` runs on an integration line (CodeFlow 3.1.1). When `check_epic_line` fails, `criteria` in `crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/ci/acceptance.rs` judges the line as a frozen task range and drops the reason (`check_epic_line(...).is_ok()`), so every completion binds at the range head. `task_landing` then names the head commit's own change as "the completion also changes <path>" (#341, 16 tasks in one run), and `later_change` diffs the whole tree from the reviewed commit to the head and names the first path in byte order, which was a file `main` brought in through a sync merge and that equals `main` (#320, 1,592 changed paths for one task). On a verified line, AC-1 binds a line completion at its line landing, which removes #320's blame for a reopened and re-completed task. AC-7 and AC-8 make the downgrade and the comparison visible, and pin #320's shape.

TSK-434.title: An integration branch can be deleted only after it is merged
context: Operator decision of 2026-10-22: agents should be able to delete an integration branch, but only after it is merged. Today `codeflow hook git-guard` allows `git push origin --delete integration/EPC-099-test` (exit 0) with no merge check, and the pre-push hook's deletion rule covers protected refs only (`git.delete_protected`, `crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/git_guard.rs:8681-8688` and `git_hook.rs:890-895`); the only thing that stops the deletion is the deletion rule in GitHub's "Integration hosted gates" ruleset, a remote setting outside the guards. The cleanup rule TSK-402 widens is instruction text (`worktrees.md`), not enforcement, and TSK-421's line close lists a deletion without performing it.

Outcome: **git-guard and the pre-push hook refuse deleting a remote or local `integration/**` branch unless the branch is fully contained in its target, there is no open pull request from or into it, and it is not a protected branch; a refusal names the missing proof, an allowed deletion names the proof it checked, and protected branches and release tags stay refused.**
Rules:

items.text: **Containment** is ancestry on the fetched target: the branch tip is an ancestor of `origin/<target>`, where the target is the epic's protected branch (`main`) for an epic line, read from the epic record or, with none, the repository's default branch. A target the guard cannot fetch or read is a missing proof.

**No open pull request** from or into the branch, read through the remote provider where one is configured (`codeflow remote`); where the provider cannot be asked, the proof is missing and the deletion refuses, naming the route (ask a person, or configure the provider).
**Protected branches and release tags** (`main`, `master`, the policy globs, and tags the release policy names) keep today's `git.delete_protected` refusal whatever the proofs say.

The same judgment covers `git push --delete`, `git push :<ref>`, `git branch -d`/`-D` of a local `integration/**` branch and the `refs/` spellings, on git-guard (the Claude, Codex and Grok planes) and on the pre-push hook; the message lists each proof with its result.
Once this task lands and is reviewed, the operator removes the deletion rule from the GitHub "Integration hosted gates" ruleset; that ruleset change stays the operator's and is not part of this task.

context: Non-goals: deleting task branches (TSK-402's cleanup rule and TSK-319 in 4.1.0); closing a line's records (TSK-421).
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 at the operator's direction of that day.

TSK-435.title: Records state their Outcome and epics their Deliverables
context: Operator decision of 2026-10-22, part of the issue #280 work: an explicit Outcome on records, and Deliverables on epics. Issue 280 asks that an epic state one value line ("after this merges, X can do Y"); today the task template has no home for it (records put an "Outcome:" sentence in the Description by convention), the epic template has no Deliverables section, and `codeflow validate --docs` checks a task's Deliverables (`crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/record_text.rs:581-596`) but no Outcome anywhere.

Outcome: **after this lands, a task or epic record created with the templates carries an `## Outcome` section with one line saying what someone can do once it lands, an epic carries a `## Deliverables` section like a task's, `codeflow validate --docs` requires the Outcome section on records created after the change, and existing records stay valid: closed records are never changed or flagged, and an open record created before the change gets a warning, not a refusal, and gains the section when next amended.**
Rules:

items.text: **Templates.** `assets/base/pm/task.md.tmpl` and `epic.md.tmpl` gain `## Outcome` (one line, in the form "after this merges, X can do Y") between the Description and the Deliverables; `epic.md.tmpl` gains `## Deliverables` with the task template's comment. `codeflow task new` and `epic new` write both.

**Validation, adoption-aware.** The compatibility boundary is the project's own adoption of this release, identified by record identity, never by a calendar date: when `codeflow update` first brings a release that has the section, it writes the adoption marker into the project's configuration (provisional `records.outcome_required_since` in `.codeflow/project.toml`) with the adoption commit (the project's HEAD at that update) and the `uid` of every task and epic record present in the working tree at that moment, committed or not. A record is "present at adoption" when its uid is in that list; every other record is "later". A later non-terminal record whose Outcome section is missing or empty is refused by `validate --docs`; a present-at-adoption record without it gets a warning naming the section and gains the section when next amended, whatever its `created` date, so a record made with the old release the morning of a same-day upgrade stays valid; a record whose status is terminal (complete, cancelled, archived) is never flagged. A fresh `codeflow init` writes the marker with an empty list, so every record of a new project needs the section. With no marker (a project updated by hand, or one that has not yet run `codeflow update`), every missing section warns and nothing refuses, and `codeflow doctor` says the marker is missing and how `update` writes it.
**Compatibility.** No existing record is edited by this task; the "Outcome:" sentence convention in Descriptions stays valid for old records.
**Guidance.** `cf-plan` and `cf-method` "Planning an epic" name the section as the home of the value line; TSK-419's sizing guidance points at it, so TSK-419 depends on this task.

context: Non-goals: rewording existing records (TSK-418's class covers that when a project wants it); any new field in frontmatter.
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 at the operator's direction of that day.

TSK-436.title: A task criterion can record a deferred result proved after merge
context: Issue #287. A task's acceptance block accepts only `verified` or `waived` per criterion; `deferred` exists only for an epic's after-release criteria (`cf-method/references/project-organization.md`, the `deferred | owner; window; follow-up` form, read by `crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/record_text.rs:1533-1546`), and a `waived` result needs a planning amendment of that criterion inside the reviewed commit. Some criteria can only be proved after the merge: an adopter's dependency-admission check runs as `pull_request_target`, so the base's checker judges the head's data and a pull request that adds a new exception kind cannot go green until it is merged; the first push scan of `main` after the merge is the real proof. The author must reword the criterion to match local evidence, or the maintainer merges on known reds with no record that a check is owed.

Outcome: **a task's acceptance block can record a criterion as `deferred`, naming the event that will prove it, who checks it and a follow-up, with no planning amendment because the criterion does not change; `codeflow ci` and `orient` show the owed follow-up until someone records the result as verified, or as failed with a linked task.**
Rules:

items.text: **Form.** The task result reuses the epic form: `AC-n: deferred | event: <the proving event>; owner: <who checks>; follow-up: <TSK-NNN or another permitted durable record, an epic criterion or a feedback item>`. The event is free text, the owner a role or seat, the follow-up a tracked record that exists in the repository. A tracked record never cites a coordination ledger id (`FU-NNN`, `LN-NNN`, `WS-NNN`): the ledger is clone-local and absent in CI (ADR-0086), so a ledger item may link outward to the task's deferred criterion, and the durable reference stays in the record.

**Binding.** A deferred result binds like a verified one: the task can complete and land, and the block names the reviewed commit. The task stays `complete`; the deferred criteria are listed in the task's Closeout as owed.

**Resolution.** `codeflow task status <id> defer-resolve AC-n --verified <evidence>` or `--failed --task TSK-NNN` (provisional verb) appends the result under the block as a dated line, a records-only change `codeflow ci` accepts in a planning amendment or a task PR, judged like the amendment note of SPC-013 R-50. A failed result must link an open task.

**Surfacing.** `codeflow ci` prints each owed deferred result of the tasks in its range as a note, and `orient` lists every owed deferred result of the project with its event and owner, from the records alone; neither blocks and neither reads the ledger.
An epic closes only when every deferred task result is resolved, or the epic's own block defers the criterion as today.

context: Non-goals: changing `waived`; deferring a journey criterion; a hosted check that records the result by itself.
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 under the operator's decision of that day (project-management changes go in 3.2.0).

TSK-437.title: Each seat reaches only its own lane's sockets and never the container runtime
context: Issue #286, item 1. Parallel lanes each run local helper services (a browser automation server, a dev database, a preview server), and anything that can connect to a lane's service can act through it; a browser server can read files the browser reaches and take raw DevTools commands. Every seat, hook and tool runs as one OS user who also owns the container runtime socket, so a project cannot keep one lane away from another's service by changing the service alone. The shipped postures set `dangerously_allow_all_unix_sockets = false` for `cf-guard` and `cf-builder` (`assets/base/codex/config.toml:205`, `:242`) with no per-seat allowance, and the Claude presets carry no `allowUnixSockets` list; the container runtime socket is not denied by name on any plane. Two research passes agreed the criterion "no other process under the same host user may connect" cannot be met on a single-user host; this task delivers what the seat postures can.

Outcome: **a seat's sandbox can be given access to its own lane's unix sockets only, through a documented and tested per-seat launch override (Codex `unix_sockets` rules, Claude `allowUnixSockets`), and every seat denies the container runtime socket by default, with unsandboxed retries off for a seat that holds a socket allowance.**

Criteria to establish first, recorded in the task's pull request (the issue's "not verified" items): whether a per-lane Codex `unix_sockets` rule works as a launch override on the supported release, and Claude's `allowUnixSockets` default and merge behaviour on macOS. Each AC below states what the answer changes.
Non-goals: the optional supervisor and the separate-account guidance (TSK-438 in EPC-024); the services themselves, which stay the project's (unix socket, peer credentials, per-run secret).
Added by the EPC-022 amendment of 2026-10-22 under the operator's rule of 2026-10-18 (a security gap in the seat postures CodeFlow owns).

TSK-449.title: Push and CI gates stop rerunning unchanged work
context: The push and hosted CI rerun checks on unchanged work. TSK-450.title: Commit and PR style rules warn and the audit weighs severity
context: Style rules and the dependency audit cost retries and stalls without protecting a boundary. The description limit, body shape and count, unlisted trailers, en and em dashes and the PR Summary shape refuse commits and PR edits (`crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/standards.rs:172-200, 266-350, 546-590`; `crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/ci/pr_body.rs:1160-1270`); only the type, the breaking marker and the subject length feed a machine. The dependency audit fails the security review job on any advisory with no severity threshold (`.github/workflows/codeflow-ci.yml:1372-1485`); a medium advisory in a dev lockfile and the tokio advisory each stopped every PR. Seven policy keys (`security.script_bypass`, `interpreter_scan`, `enforcement_baseline`, `workflow_pushes`, `sandbox_retry`, `sandbox_retry_allow` and `git.clean_regenerable`) have no consumer in the crates and `docs/policy-reference.md:891` says the sandbox keys are not read yet. Source: the operator approved process audit of 2026-10-23, including the operator's decision of that day on the dependency audit (line numbers at `c9993bcf3`).

Scope: (1) Move to warn: description over 50, body shape and count, unlisted trailers, `policy_characters` and the PR Summary shape (a level for the description limit may need a new key; place it per `policy_key_placement`). Stay at block: commit type, the breaking marker, subject 72, `ai_attribution` (an AI trailer is still refused, though other unlisted trailers only warn), emoji, secrets, branch prefix, the `Task:` line, required PR sections and the release-impact job. The `ai_attribution` refusal message names the Claude setting that turns the host's trailer off (`includeCoAuthoredBy` and `attribution`), and the shipped settings keep both off. (2) The dependency audit follows one precedence table, used here, in the criteria and in EPC-022 AC-126. An advisory is "new" when its identity (advisory id, package, ecosystem) is in the head scan and not in the base scan. Rows apply in order: (a) a scan that fails or is incomplete is missing evidence and fails the job at both `block` and `warn`; (b) an advisory matched by a trusted suppression that has not expired passes and is reported; (c) a new advisory of any severity, low and informational included, fails; (d) a critical or high advisory fails unless a trusted triage entry (owner, rationale, expiry) states that it is not reachable, and unknown or missing reachability evidence counts as reachable; (e) a medium advisory fails unless a trusted triage entry (owner, rationale, expiry) exists and has not expired; (f) a low or informational advisory that is not new is printed and passes. There is no dev-only exemption. Composition: `security_review` and `dep_audit` share the one table and the effective level is the stricter of the two; at `block` a failing advisory row fails the job; at `warn` the same advisory rows print as warnings and the job passes; a failed or incomplete scan fails the job at both `block` and `warn`; at `off` the audit does not run. Suppressions and triage entries are read from the base commit only. The same table is mirrored by the shipped template step (this task owns `assets/base/ci/codeflow-ci.yml`'s audit step). (3) The seven unread keys leave the shipped policy, the schema and `docs/policy-reference.md`; a policy file that still sets one keeps loading. (4) `codeflow policy` prints a report of effective values.

Non-goals: no hook, guard, secret scan or remote rule changes. Protection lost by (2): a low or informational advisory that is not new, a medium advisory with a valid trusted triage entry, and a critical or high advisory with a trusted not-reachable triage entry no longer stop a merge; all are still printed on every run and the weekly scan. A medium advisory without a triage entry still fails, and so does any new advisory.

Effect on adopting projects: shipped style defaults match the intent (advisory style, blocking semantics); adopters that set the seven removed keys see them ignored with a notice, and the shipped template's audit follows the same severity rule when `dep_audit` is `block`.

Owned files: `assets/base/policy.json` and `.codeflow/policy.json` (all lines but `test_gate_on_push`, which TSK-449 owns), `hooks/standards.rs`, `hooks/policy.rs`, `hooks/policy_schema.rs`, `security/privilege.rs` where it names a removed key, `crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/policy.rs`, the Summary shape and `policy_characters` hunks of `ci/pr_body.rs` and `ci.rs`, `docs/policy-reference.md` (but the `test_gate_on_push` row), the dependency audit step of the security review job in `codeflow-ci.yml`, `osv-scanner.toml`, the shipped audit step in `assets/base/ci/codeflow-ci.yml`, a new audit script under `scripts/` with its test, the shipped Claude settings under `assets/base/settings/` and `.claude/settings.json`. The last-release fixtures are not edited. The Reviews and release-impact hunks of `pr_body.rs` are TSK-451.
