TSK-1091.title: The anchor refusal names the branch shape a new standalone record needs
TSK-1091.about: After this merges, an author whose standalone record is refused for its branch name is told the branch shape the record needs and how to get there, from `codeflow ci`, `codeflow work start` and the pre-push hook alike.
context: Source: issue #430 (CodeFlow 3.1.1, filed 2026-10-30 by an adopter), triaged the same day. No open task covers it; TSK-414 (complete) covers only a cancelled standalone record landing through a `plan/` branch.

A pull request adds a standalone task record on a branch whose name does not carry the task (`chore/close-tsk-nnn-record`), with `Task: TSK-NNN` in its body. `codeflow ci` refuses it with `work.stable_planning_anchor`: "task TSK-NNN is not present at the merge-base; land its epic planning record, or carry its own standalone record on this task branch", and the remedy says to run `codeflow work start`. The record is on the branch, and `work start` only checks the anchor, so neither tells the author what to change. The same range passes on a branch named `chore/TSK-NNN-<slug>`.

The cause, read on the line tip `b7ae7c6a6`: `standalone_at_head` (`crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/work_start.rs:2232`) accepts a record that is not at the merge-base only when the branch's work suffix starts with `TSK-NNN-`, and otherwise returns `TaskNotAnchored`, whose text (`work_start.rs:69`) does not mention the branch. Its remedy, `WORK_START_MERGE_PLANNING` (`crates/codeflow-core/src/remedy.rs:340`), names `codeflow work start`. `TaskNotAnchored` also covers a record missing from both the merge-base and the head, and an epic task whose planning has not landed.
The verdicts stay as they are: the rule is right, and only its text and remedy change. Non-goals: accepting a record on a branch that does not carry the task.

TSK-1092.title: A refused interpreter that names an enforcement path says what it found and names the read route
TSK-1092.about: After this merges, an agent refused for naming an enforcement path in an interpreter is told whether the code or an argument named it and how to read the file instead.
context: Source: issue #431 (CodeFlow 3.1.1, filed 2026-10-30 by an adopter), triaged the same day. A reviewer computing the digest of a managed workflow with `python3 -I -c "...open('.github/workflows/codeflow-ci.yml','rb')..."` was refused under `git.hook_integrity` with the remedy "the enforcement hooks and their policy are not agent-editable", which speaks of an edit the reviewer never tried. A read of `.codeflow/policy.json` the same way got the same text.

The verdicts stay: an inline program cannot be shown to be read-only, so the guard keeps failing closed. What changes is what the refusal says. Read on the line tip `b7ae7c6a6`, whose binary already differs from 3.1.1 here (TSK-302 landed):

items.text: `interpreter.rs` runs TSK-302's argument reader first (`crates/codeflow-core/src/security/interpreter.rs:38`, `arguments::evaluate`), which reports every word after the interpreter, a `-c` code string included, as "an interpreter argument `<path>` may reach `repository enforcement files`" with the `INTERPRETER_ARGUMENT` remedy (`crates/codeflow-core/src/security/arguments.rs:197`, `crates/codeflow-core/src/remedy.rs:461`), which names `cat`, `jq`, `grep` and a stdin redirect.

The broader literal scan that follows (`interpreter.rs:94-110`) reports "interpreter code names the enforcement path" with the edit-only `HOOK_INTEGRITY` remedy (`remedy.rs:457`), but exec-guard keeps the first finding of equal strength for one rule (`crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/exec_guard.rs:322`, `merge_strongest`), so on the line the argument finding is the one printed. The issue's digest command, fed to the line binary on stdin and never run, prints the argument text and the read routes.
3.1.1, which the issue ran, has no argument reader for this case and prints the code finding with the edit-only remedy.

context: So the line's defect is attribution: a path inside `-c` code is called an argument, and the edit-only text is still reachable wherever the argument reader does not fire first. The read routes are a plain reader (`cat`, `jq`, `grep`, `shasum`, `git show <ref>:<path>`) and a redirect into the program's stdin, where the shell opens the file read-only.
Non-goals: judging an obvious read in code as a read (the issue's second option, which a later reopen of the path defeats); any verdict change.

TSK-1093.title: Work claim adopts the agent's own checked-out task branch and publishes it
TSK-1093.about: After this merges, an agent that built a task on its own unpushed task branch ahead of the claim can claim the task from that branch and publish it as the claim, while every other carrier still refuses.
context: Source: issue #433 (CodeFlow 3.1.1, filed 2026-10-30 by an adopter), triaged the same day. An agent built an epic task ahead of its claim on the local branch `task/TSK-150-<slug>`, never pushed. Run from that worktree, `codeflow work claim TSK-150` refused: "TSK-150 is already claimed by a visible branch: task/TSK-150-...", naming the branch the agent was on. No remote branch carried the task, the name was the one the claim would create, and the branch contained the target's tip. The refusal names no route, so an agent either stops or works around the claim's create-only push.
Read on the line tip `b7ae7c6a6`, in `crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/readiness.rs`:

items.text: `visible_work_branches` (`:350`) counts local branches as claims, as `.codeflow/rules/worktrees.md:66` documents.

`claim_on` (`:1743`) drops the current branch from the carriers only on the standalone route (`standalone_claim_base`, `:1709`; the `retain` at `:1787`), which renames a branch holding a new standalone record. An epic task, or a record already on the target, never takes it.
Every other carrier that has not landed refuses (`:1793`).
`work start` already reports other carriers as information, not a refusal (`crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/work.rs:408`).

context: Rule: `work claim` adopts the current branch only when all of these hold, and refuses otherwise with the reason and a route:

items.text: the branch is checked out in the worktree the command runs in;
it is the only carrier of the id among local branches and every remote the claim reads; any remote carrier refuses;
its name is the name the claim would create;
it is not a protected branch;

it contains the claim's base: the stack base of the `--on` pins when they are given (`stack_base`, the base a new claim is cut from, `readiness.rs:1756`), otherwise the target's tip; with valid pins the target may have moved past the branch;
readiness is judged on the target's record, as for a new claim.

context: With an `origin` remote it then publishes the branch with the existing create-only push (`--force-with-lease=<destination>:`, `readiness.rs:1815`) and prints "adopted" instead of "created"; a lost push race refuses and leaves local and remote refs unchanged. Without `origin` it adopts the branch locally and says the claim is visible only in this clone, as a new claim does today (`crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/work.rs:292`).

The claim is the mark other agents trust to see who holds a task, so the review carries the `cf-security-reviewer` checklist. Today's refusal stays when another clone has pushed a branch for the id or a second local branch carries it.

TSK-1095.title: codeflow status --json gives percent complete, location, order, lanes, windows and issues for any scope
TSK-1095.about: After this merges, anyone on an adopting project can run `codeflow status` with a scope and get, for a task, an epic or the whole line, the percent complete at each level with its basis, what is on `main` and what is not with the path to `main`, the order of work, the lanes carrying it, a window per item and milestone with its basis, and the issues per item, each fact live or marked unverified, as text and JSON.
context: The operator asked on 2026-10-30 for a command or skill that reports the status of work properly each time it is asked, in any project that adopts CodeFlow: what is being worked on with just the right context, the epics and tasks involved, percent complete at each level (the epic, the task and the overall scope), the lanes a coordinator runs and the overall across them, the order work is done in, the expected time to completion for each item, and the issues for each item. On 2026-10-30 (20:40) the operator added that timing must read at a glance on a real time axis, and that work landed on an integration line counts as done while the report makes clear what is on `main`, what is not, and when it gets there. Nothing computes this today: `codeflow status` prints counts from the working tree with no JSON (`crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/status.rs:7-17`), `work next` prints readiness (`crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/readiness.rs:27-48`), and `report ceremony` is the only report (`crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/report.rs:17-22`). Every session writes its own status by hand, with the stale facts the writing rule warns about.

This task is the engine: it extends `codeflow status`, the command an adopter already reaches for, with the facts and a JSON form. TSK-1098 renders them as the figure-led `cf-present` document (`--present`) and the plain-text form (`--md`); TSK-1099 is the `cf-status` skill that answers a status request with them. TSK-312 (`status --json` on TSK-311's fact model) is merged into this task on 2026-10-31 and cancelled; every TSK-312 criterion is kept below (AC-2, AC-7 and AC-11). Shape decided in planning, open to the builder's investigation (AC-1):

Figure: the scope selects records, git and the optional forge, ledger and session file supply facts, and the percent, location, order, lane, window and issue views are derived from them; nothing is stored.
Decisions, each reversible and disclosed here:

items.text: **Command and flags.** `codeflow status` keeps its text view unchanged with no flag. New: `--json`; the scope flags `--task TSK-NNN`, `--epic EPC-NNN` (repeatable) and `--line <integration branch>`, with the default scope every open epic whose home is the current target; a scope flag with no output flag prints the progress text view. `--json`, `--present <path>` (TSK-1098) and `--md` (TSK-1098) are mutually exclusive output choices over the same facts; `--session <file>` and `--since <previous facts file>` are optional input modifiers: this task defines the `--session` schema and merges its facts into the lanes view, and reads a previous `--json` output through `--since` to emit what changed (landings, new red checks, tasks added, blockers opened or cleared, decisions recorded) with their times. "Overall" is the named scope, so a task report shows the task, its epic and that epic's place in the scope. The coordinator recommended this shape on 2026-10-30 over a new `report` verb; the operator confirms the names at plan approval.

**Stage ladder.** A task's percent is the highest stage it has reached on a fixed ladder printed with every report: not started 0, in progress (a claim or a task branch with commits) 20, in review (an open pull request) 50, reviewed (an approving other-lineage review on the head) 75, landed on its home target 100; cancelled tasks are excluded from every denominator and listed. Criteria verified against criteria total is shown beside the stage percent from the acceptance block when one exists, never mixed with it, labelled `criteria`, bound to the reviewed SHA the block names and marked `stale` when the head has moved since; a block or count that is absent is `not recorded`, never `0 of N`. An epic's percent is the mean of its open and complete tasks' stage percents, with the count of tasks per stage beside it; the scope's percent is the same over its unique tasks, never a mean of epic percents. An empty denominator or an unreadable record is `unknown`, never 0 or 100.

**Location and the path to main.** Landed on the integration line is done for the task percent, and each task and epic also carries a location from its own landing evidence: `main` (its landing commit reachable from the trusted remote's default branch), `line` (reachable from its integration line only), `pull request` (an open pull request into the line or into `main`), `branch` (a task branch with commits and no pull request) or `none`; a checkpoint merge of the line into `main` moves only the tasks whose landing commits it carries, never the epic as a whole. A task whose record is on the line but whose work has not started is `none` with the note `record on line`, never `line`. A `pull request` location carries its substate (`draft`, `open`, `approved at <sha>` with the reviewed SHA named and marked `not the head` when the head moved); "ready" is never a location, it is the next step's word. The open pull requests into `main` are listed with the task state of each, so a lead can say "no 4.0.0 pull request into `main` is open; the only open one is for a cancelled task" rather than an absolute none. Every remote claim is bound to the fetched ref identity it was read from (the SHA and the fetch time) and marked `unverified` when that ref is older than the sweep interval or could not be fetched. The epic's path to `main` is the remaining steps on the landing route the project records (land the open units on the line, the line's full gate, the pull request to `main`, the operator's merge, release when the project has a release step); an agent-owned step carries a window from the scenarios; an operator-owned step is two events, ready for the operator (a window) and done by the operator (undated, `awaiting the operator`), and every step after it is conditional on it and says so. The hop to `main` always carries its condition in words and, when the scenarios give one, the earliest conditional end under the intake-stops scenario ("after the epic is complete on the line, earliest about N days if intake stops and capacity holds; then the operator's merge"), so "when does it reach `main`" has an answer beyond "no date"; this is a read of record and git state, never a promise.

**Named sets.** The fact model defines each named set once and every view reuses it: the landing chain (the open pull requests into the line in landing order, with the landed ones and their times), each lane's tasks, the path to `main`; a count of a set is the count of that one definition.

**Order.** A topological order of `depends_on` among the scope's open tasks, authoritative: a task never precedes its predecessor. Among tasks with no dependency between them the state decides the place: active first (claimed or started, through the readiness core `work next` uses, after TSK-1038 never offering landed work), then ready, then waiting with the predecessor waited on, then blocked with the reason; so a blocked predecessor sits before its waiting successor, and the state is printed on every row. The critical path is the chain whose planning-scenario durations sum highest, marked, and the longest chain by count is reported apart as the dependency depth, never called critical.

**Lanes.** When the coordination ledger has lanes (TSK-439, when landed), each lane with its scope, attempt, seat kind and the task's percent; otherwise observed lanes: each claimed or started task with its worktree, branch, open pull request and head age, labelled `observed`, with no seat and no owner invented. A `--session <file>` of session-only facts (lane, task, builder, reviewer, seat, verdict in flight, blocker, each with its observation time) is validated against a shipped schema, merged into the lanes view labelled `session`, and never changes a percent or a stage. A project with no ledger and no session file shows "lanes: observed only".

**Windows.** Every open agent-owned item and every agent-owned step on the path to `main` carries one window: the earliest and latest end as durations from the snapshot time (the as-of moment), with the planning value inside it, and a start that is the as-of moment or its predecessors' latest end, so a renderer can place it as a band on one time axis with the as-of rule. A blocked item's window is conditional on its blocker clearing and says so; an item whose window has no honest basis (an unknown predecessor, an undated operator step before it, a cancelled or unreadable predecessor) is `not yet estimable` with the reason, never a number. When the project has adopted `cf-estimate` and a forecast record covers the scope, the windows come from it, bound to the scope and revision it estimated and marked stale when criteria changed since. Otherwise the window comes from the planned throughput rule (`cf-method/references/workflow-lifecycle.md` "Planned work moves at speed": at least one task per build lane per hour, preferably two): earliest at two tasks per lane-hour with one review and landing cycle of one hour per unit, planning at one per lane-hour with one review cycle and one repair round, latest at one per lane-hour with two review rounds and one landing cycle per batch, over the open tasks along the order with the number of lanes observed. Every window carries a `basis_kind`: `forecast` (an adopted forecast record), `observed` (the planned rate over the lanes observed) or `assumed` (no lane observed, so one lane is assumed and the window is labelled `assumed one lane` wherever it is drawn, never mixed with an observed window). The scope's finish is forecast under two named scenarios in one place: intake stops (the open tasks at the planning rate) and intake continues at the rate observed over the last seven days (which may give no finite finish, said in words). Each window prints its basis and computation time, is a duration from the as-of moment and never a calendar commitment, and the planned-throughput rate is never lowered to an observed slow pace.

**Issues.** Per task: blocked (reason, owner, revisit), waiting (the predecessor), an open pull request whose required check is red, missing or pending (read through the ledger's bounded observer `crates/codeflow-core/src/coord/observe.rs`, `unverified` when offline), stale (claimed with no commit for longer than the sweep interval `[sweep] interval_minutes`, default 30), a deferred acceptance result owed (TSK-436), and a follow-up awaiting the operator when the ledger is present. Each issue names its unblocker (an agent lane, a CI run, a predecessor, the operator) and the window in which it is expected to clear when the scenarios give one, so a renderer can draw a blocked list and an explicit "needs the operator" set. The operator set is `none owed` only when every source that can name an owed item (records, the ledger when present, the away activation's owed items and decisions when an activation exists (TSK-1045, read with its own coverage result and never written), the forge through the observer, the session file when given) was checked at this snapshot; otherwise it is `not established` with the unchecked or unreadable source named, never an all-clear. Per lane: a seat with no progress since the last tick, from ledger or session evidence only.

**Pace and intake.** Over the scope's history the fact model gives, per day for the last seven days and in total, the tasks landed on their home target, the tasks added to the scope (from record creation dates and merge times, each named) and the open count at the end of each day, with the lane count observed, so a reader can see whether intake outruns landing. Two rates are given and labelled: the scope's own observed landing rate, and the planned capacity rate over the lanes observed (the planned-throughput rule); the finish forecast names which rate each scenario uses, and the intake-stops count names the tasks added since the previous snapshot as intake. This is the basis line of the windows and is printed with them.

**Fact model.** JSON with `schema_version`, a snapshot time with its zone, and every field present with `unknown` or `unverified` rather than omitted or zero, frozen by a schema test; each measure (percents, locations, order, lanes, windows, issues, pace) carries an `evidence` entry naming its source (records, git, the forge through the observer, the ledger, the activation, a forecast record, the session file), its check time and whether it was checked, so a renderer can draw the evidence matrix. Every forge observation keeps its read time and is never overwritten by a later one without its own read time; every time in the model carries one zone, the snapshot's, and a check state is the value read (`skipped` and `missing` stay so, never rewritten as `running`). Every snapshot carries the repository identity TSK-311's envelope defines, so a `--since` file from another repository is refused even when its display ids match. TSK-311's `report program` reuses this model for the records it adds cross-line home and currency to, and its AC-4's "schema test that TSK-312 reuses" reads as this task's schema test. This task reads records through the existing readiness core and record store (`crates/codeflow-core/src/status.rs`, `workgraph/readiness.rs`) and never adds a second record reader.

**Report facts the operator asked for on 2026-10-31.** The operator's standing requirements for every report (deliverable and overall percent; each epic or topic with what it is, done and not done, the reasoning and the percent; blockers with a recommended action, why and alternatives; operator inputs with context, options, recommendation and reasoning; commands that run from any folder) need facts the model did not name. The fact model carries, per scope, the `deliverable` (the epic's `## Outcome` line, or the task's, `not recorded` when absent) beside the percent; per epic, `what_it_is` (its Outcome line), the `done` and `not_done` task lists and a `reasoning` line (the stage counts and the basis the percent is computed from); `themes` grouping an epic's tasks by the record section that introduced them (the amendment heading, which is how this repository's epics group asks) or by a `theme:` line in the task record when present, `ungrouped` otherwise, so a renderer can drill from the epic to a theme to a task; per issue, `recommended_action`, `why` and `alternatives` filled from the record (the `## Blocker` reason, owner and revisit, the follow-ups, a decision note) or from the `--session` file labelled `session`, and `not recorded` when neither has them, never invented; per operator item, a `decision` with `context`, `options`, `recommendation` and `reasoning` from the same sources with the same rule; and per task the `context` facts a drill-down needs (outcome line, location, lane, state, window, last moved, open pull request). Every command the model cites (a check to rerun, a pull request to open, a log to read) carries the repository's absolute path or a `git -C <path>` form so a script assembled from them runs from any folder; the renderer (TSK-1098) assembles the script.

context: Non-goals: rendering (TSK-1098); the skill and its wiring (TSK-1099); cross-line home and currency (TSK-311); a scheduler, daemon or stored report; writing to any record or ledger; a check or verdict (the report never fails a gate); tracked class and lane vocabulary (TSK-313, TSK-314, EPC-023).

TSK-1096.title: Present and portal tables encode state, extent and emphasis from one grammar module
TSK-1096.about: After this merges, an author or a generator can show state, magnitude, grouping and emphasis inside a table on the present surface and the docs portal, readable at a glance and without colour, with every exact value still present as text.

next.reason: task TSK-1096 depends on TSK-445, whose anchored status is 'todo', not complete

context: The operator's clarification of 2026-10-30 (20:15, relayed by the coordinator): avoiding text tables does not mean banning tables; it means that when a table is the better shape, it is presented visually, with colour encodings, inline bars, status marks, grouping and emphasis, never as plain text. The feedback of the same day (20:40) added that a table must be easy to consume and look good, elegant and restrained, never cheesy or overdone, and that a disclosure must open to content presented as well as the first reading path, since layering information is not sweeping text into a box the reader fears to open. Neither surface can do this today:

items.text: the present `table` block holds string cells rendered as Markdown in plain `<td>` elements (`crates/codeflow-present/src/render.rs:406-425`; schema `.codeflow/schemas/present/document-v2.schema.json`, `table`), with no state, bar, tone or group a cell can carry;

the present `status` block draws pass and fail with the same filled mark and pending and not-run with the same outlined mark, told apart by colour alone, and hides the mark from assistive technology without emitting the state as text (`crates/codeflow-present/src/render.rs:425-440`, `crates/codeflow-present/web/src/styles.css`, the `.state-mark` rules), against the two-channel rule the figure grammar sets for every pair of states (`figure-grammar.md` section 2, rule 3);

the portal renders Markdown tables as Starlight tables and its generated capability table prints status as plain text (`assets/docs-portal/starter/scripts/adapter.mjs:422`, `scripts/lib.mjs:1150`); the lookup wrappers in `portal.css:688-762` change layout at phone width only;
the figure twin is an exact textual fallback, which must stay as it is (`crates/codeflow-present/web/src/figure-grammar.mjs`, the twin renderer).

context: Outcome: **one encoded-table vocabulary, drawn by the grammar module both runtimes load, lets an author or a generator give a table cell a state mark from the mark vocabulary, an inline extent bar against a declared maximum, a tone (accent, cat1, cat2) or an emphasis, and a row a group, so the present `table` block and a declared portal table read as visuals with their exact values kept as text; the present `status` block meets the two-channel rule with an accessible state name; and the figure twin stays the plain fallback.**
Figure: one vocabulary and one module serve both surfaces; each surface keeps its own carrier and shell.
Decisions, each reversible and disclosed here:

items.text: A cell is a string (as today) or an object with `text` and any of `state` (a mark from `figure-grammar.md` section 4, drawn with its two non-hue channels and its name as accessible text), `bar` (`value`, `max`, optional `unit` and `label` naming what is measured, such as `criteria`; drawn to length on the table's one declared scale per column, the value kept as text beside it; a `value` of null draws no bar and the text `not recorded`, never zero), `tone` (`accent`, `cat1`, `cat2`; hue only, never the only carrier) and `strong`; a row may carry `group`, drawn as a group heading. A legend lists every state and tone used, as figures do. The present `table` block gains these fields under `schema_version: 2` without breaking a string-only table.

The portal carrier is a declared table bound in `portal.config.json` like a figure (`tables`, with `route` and `panel` or `anchor`), drawn by the adapter from a declaration file; a Markdown table in a source stays a Markdown table. The builder confirms in AC-1 that a declaration beats a `cf-table` fence in sources under the content contract, and records the choice; the vocabulary is the same either way.

An encoded table is a primary carrier when a comparison or lookup is its better shape; the method text that puts tables in disclosures (TSK-445 AC-3) applies to reference detail, and TSK-1097 restates the rule.

No new colours: the `--cf-fig-*` roles and the mark vocabulary draw everything; a status cell is the `cov`, `part`, `notrun`, `na`, `nc`, `done`, `todo`, `blocked` or `stop` mark, and the `status` block's four states map to `done` (pass), `stop` (fail), `todo` (pending) and `notrun` (not run), each with the state name in the accessible tree.

Restraint is part of the vocabulary: a column carries one encoding (a mark, a bar or a tone), a table uses at most two tones beside the accent, bars share one scale per column, row striping and borders come from the kit's `chrome.css` table rules and never from the declaration, and the legend lists only what is used; the renderer refuses a cell with two encodings and a table with more than three tones. The kit's table rule in `chrome.css` sets the quiet surface (hairline rules, tabular numerals, a group heading one step heavier), so an encoded table looks the same on both surfaces.

An encoded table and the figure families are the carriers inside a disclosure too: the present `disclosure` block and the portal's details panels accept the same blocks as the first reading path, and the twin of a figure stays the exact accessible fallback and writes every mark as its human word (`checked`, `partial`, `not run`, `not applicable`, `not claimed`, `unknown`), never its identifier. The runtime's own figure Details panel, which today opens to the description paragraph and the plain twin (`crates/codeflow-present/web/src/figure-grammar.mjs`, the `Details` renderer near line 722, and the portal's copy), is the disclosure the operator met: it opens instead to a one-line lead and the twin drawn as an encoded table (states as marks, values with bars where the figure drew extent), with the plain twin kept beneath for assistive readers and copy, on both surfaces. A disclosure's closed summary line may carry a `state` mark and a `count` chip, so a closed disclosure says what is inside and how much (the design brief revision 2, gap 8).

The vocabulary gains an `unknown` mark (a hatched ring with the word), distinct from `na` (faint, not applicable) and `notrun` (hatch), so a generator can draw a value it could not establish without calling it inapplicable or zero.

context: Non-goals: new figure families; a table that replaces a figure where a relationship carries the point (the altitude contract stands); the portal page rewrites (TSK-446); the method text beyond the block selection table (TSK-1097); product or brand design.

TSK-1097.title: The present and portal craft meets the immediately obvious bar, with the artifact guidance adopted
TSK-1097.about: After this merges, an author of a present document or a portal page has one checkable bar for information that is immediately obvious, both runtimes warn on the parts a machine can measure, and the figure guidance carries the chart lessons the utility was missing.

next.reason: task TSK-1097 depends on TSK-445, whose anchored status is 'todo', not complete

context: The operator's principle of 2026-10-30 (20:15, relayed by the coordinator) for `cf-present` and `cf-docs-portal` alike: information that is immediately obvious, visual plus supporting text, with the right context, a leading anchor and an order that spares the reader from connecting the dots; visuals and colour used in useful ways that convey things faster without losing detail or the real complexity. The operator also asked for Anthropic's artifact guidance (artifact-design, artifact-diagramming and dataviz, read on 2026-10-30) to be compared with the two skills and its good parts adopted. TSK-445 (PR 344) already carries the method's anchor, section leads, figure-first order and the artifact-design and diagramming lessons; TSK-446 fixes the portal's page order. This task closes what neither covers and writes the principle as a checkable bar in both skills. The operator's feedback of 2026-10-30 (20:40) sharpened the bar on three points, all of which apply to `cf-present`, `cf-docs-portal` and the status report alike: a detail section is layered information and opens to content presented as well as the first path, never text swept into a box; a table that is needed is elegant and restrained; and a document or page answers the questions its reader brings, in the order they arise, so the reader never connects the dots.
Gap list against the artifact guidance, paraphrased (no text copied):

adopt: `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` on table cells, the twin and extent value labels in the kit sheets; proportional elsewhere

The figure grammar has nine families and none draws time: the method says a series over time is "a table and one sentence naming that boundary" (`explanation-method.md` stage 3), the extent family draws reach from a baseline on one scale, and the layering family draws planes over one shared axis of moments with no durations (`figure-grammar.md` section 1). Outcome: **a tenth family, `schedule`, drawn by the grammar module both runtimes load, places items as windows on one time axis (a band from the earliest to the latest end with a soft fill and a dashed outline, no solid part, the planning value a thin tick inside), marks the as-of moment as a vertical rule labelled `as of`, draws a completed event as a filled disc at its time, writes each dependency in words beside its band (`after 426`) and draws a connector from a predecessor's latest end to a successor's start only for a dependency the declaration marks governing, labelled with the predecessor's name, groups rows by lane or by location (`main`, integration line, pull request, branch), draws an agent-owned milestone such as the line's gate as a diamond at the end of its window, draws an operator-owned step as a readiness window ending in the human ring with the done event undated and written in words (`your decision`, `no date`) off the axis, hatches a stopped item's band with its condition (`after the issue clears`), writes `not yet estimable` with the reason for an item with no window instead of drawing it, and keeps the twelve rules (two non-hue channels per state, a legend, a one-sentence caption, a table twin with the exact windows and bases, a narrow recomposition that stacks rows and keeps the axis).**

Figure: rows are items grouped by lane or location, bands run from the earliest to the latest end with the planning tick inside, a disc is a completed event, hatching is a stopped item with its condition, connectors show dependencies, the diamond is an agent milestone, the ring is the operator's decision, and the undated merge is written off the axis.

items.text: The axis reads as a clock when the declaration's `as_of` carries a timestamp with its zone: ticks show the clock time with the zone named once in the axis title and the offset from the as-of moment (`+2 h`) beneath, at a cadence chosen from the span and the available width (two hours for a span up to a day at wide, six hours at narrow, one day for a span over two days, with the first and last tick always labelled and never more than one tick per 80 units), midnight carries its date, and the span starts before the earliest completed event so every disc sits in a labelled past; without a timestamp the axis is hours from the as-of moment, then days when a window passes 48 hours. A conditional or stopped band is drawn in relative units with its condition beside it and never as clock times, since its start is unknown. The renderer prints the basis of the windows beside the legend and a local legend of at most four entries under the figure. A second panel with a days scale may follow the same label column when a milestone lies beyond the hours span, and a lane figure that draws windows reuses this family's axis header rather than bare ticks.

Location gets a shared chip vocabulary in `figure-grammar.md` section 4, drawn by the module wherever an item appears (schedule rows, encoded table cells, flow stations): `main` (the `layer-remote` square with a check inside and a heavier outline, cat2 tone), `line` (the plain `layer-remote` square, cat1 tone), `pull request` (the `node` ring with the number), `branch` (the `optional` dashed outline), each with its word, so every pair differs on two non-hue channels (glyph and outline weight for `main` against `line`) and no page defines location by tone alone (the design brief revision 2, gap 4 and its marks section).

Marks reuse the vocabulary: `optional` (soft fill, dashed outline) for a window band, `done` for a completed event disc, `blocked` hatching for a stopped band, `trans` for a dependency connector, `merge` for an agent milestone diamond, `human` for the operator ring, `limit` for the as-of rule, with the `accent` tone on the critical path and `cat1` and `cat2` as lane companions; a new mark is added only if the builder shows the vocabulary cannot carry a state.

The declaration takes `axis` (unit and span), `as_of`, `rows` (item, group, state, a window with earliest, planning and latest, completed events with times, dependencies, kind item or milestone, owner agent or human, a condition for a stopped or conditional band, a reason for an item with no window). The field names follow the window shape TSK-1095's record specifies (earliest, planning and latest end as durations from the as-of moment, a start, a condition, a basis), so TSK-1098 can bind the facts without a translation layer; the derived binding itself (`source` into a `codeflow status --json` file) is TSK-1098's, since it needs the landed facts.
The chat form is the fenced ASCII above, under 78 columns.

context: Non-goals: a daemon or scheduler; computing the windows (TSK-1095); the progress document (TSK-1098); a Gantt editor; a calendar.

TSK-1101.title: The present export sizes each stage frame from its content and waits for stages to paint
TSK-1101.about: After this merges, an exported present page shows every stage the live session measured whole and declares every unmeasured stage with a notice at the fixed height, never a silent clip, so a review of a document with `html` stages reads what the live page shows or says where it cannot.
context: Four reviewers of the status report design brief (Fable, Codex GPT-6 Astra, Grok 4.7 and a fresh Claude Opus reader, consolidated on 2026-10-30 21:42 EDT) read the exported page and all saw the same defect: the live session hosts each `html` stage inline (`crates/codeflow-present/src/render.rs:591`, `.cf-stage-host`), but the export puts each stage in a sandboxed frame with a fixed height (`crates/codeflow-present/web/src/styles.css:651-654`, `.block--html iframe { block-size: 28rem }`), so a stage taller than the frame is clipped (a nine-row lane board showed seven rows) and a shorter one leaves a blank gap, and at phone width the frame clips again. A static capture of the export taken before the stages' script has painted shows them blank. The reviewers ruled the export a review capture only and the live session the handover surface until this is fixed, and named the fix: size the frame from the stage's rendered height. Inlining the stage, their other option, is ruled out by the ADR-0049 boundary, so the height is measured on the live page in the export's geometry; an unmeasured stage keeps the fixed height with a notice, never a silent clip.

Outcome: **an exported present page shows every measured `html` stage whole, at the height the live session measured for the export's own geometry, in light and dark and at phone width, with no clipping and no blank gap, declares any unmeasured stage instead of clipping it, and a capture of the export taken after the page reports ready shows every frame loaded.**
Figure: the live page and the export today, and the export after the fix, for a tall stage and a short one.
Decisions, each reversible and disclosed here:

items.text: The runtime boundary of ADR-0049 is unchanged: the export keeps the sandboxed `iframe` with `srcdoc`, `sandbox=""`, no `allow-scripts` and no `allow-same-origin` (`crates/codeflow-present/src/export.rs`, the `export_html_stage_keeps_content_and_sandbox` test), no script runs inside a frame, and the stage is never inlined in an export. The height comes from the live session instead, measured in the export's own geometry: the live page renders each stage a second time in a hidden measuring host that reproduces the export frame's layout (the export's content width in CSS pixels, its padding, no review rail), at each content width the export produces (its wide and narrow columns), and reports the rendered height (stage id, revision, export content width, the export rendering contract it measured under, height in CSS pixels) to the session store over the existing session channel; the live page's own inline host, whose width changes with the review rail, is never the source. The export rendering contract is a digest the binary computes over the inputs that decide a stage's rendered height in an export: the export stylesheets it embeds (`export.rs:186`, `styles.css`, `figure.css`, `export-fallback.css`), the root font size and type scale, the bundled fonts and the frame geometry; the live page reports the contract its measuring host ran under, and the export writes a stored height as the frame's block size only when the stored revision, content width and rendering contract all equal the ones it renders under, with a floor of one row and no ceiling (Codex round 8, F5: TSK-1109 of PR 449 changes the root scale and stage typography, so a height measured before it is wrong after it at the same revision and width). A stage with no matching measurement (a document never opened live at that revision, an export at another width, or a measurement under another rendering contract) is `not measured`: it keeps the present fixed height and shows a visible notice, "height not measured at this width; open the session", never a silent clip; opening the session re-measures under the current contract. The outcome is therefore: every measured stage whole, every unmeasured stage declared.

The reported height is validated input: numeric, bounded, bound to a stage id, a revision, a content width the store knows the export produces and the rendering contract digest the binary knows; a report for another revision, an unknown stage, an unlisted width or an unknown contract is dropped; a later report for the same stage, revision, content width and contract replaces the earlier one.

The export marks the document ready (`data-cf-ready` on the root) only after every frame has fired `load` or failed within a bounded wait, from the host page's own script, with a visible notice on a frame that did not load, so a capture tool can wait on one signal.
The export's chrome says what it is: a review capture of the session at a time, with the session the handover surface.

context: Non-goals: a change to the ADR-0049 boundary (no script in a frame, no inline stage in an export); the figure grammar; a new block or a schema field for height.

TSK-1102.title: The qualification runner accepts a peer in a registered fixture worktree
TSK-1102.about: After this merges, the qualification operator can run trials under the per-trial `--codex-hook-trust=bypass` option whose subject opens a Codex review seat in its task worktree, as the method prescribes: the peer reaches ready, receives its delivery and the trial finishes with no validity flag from it; under the default `review` option such a peer is still refused at its hook screen; and the runner still refuses any peer whose working directory fails the stated identity checks at any moment it looks.
context: The native qualification runner (`evals/qualification/runner.py`) refuses every peer seat a subject opens outside the fixture repository root: `check_peer_state` compares the peer's working directory with the fixture path and raises "peers start in the fixture repository" (runner.py:1302-1303 at TSK-1094's reviewed head `addf25865`). The method puts a review seat in the subject's task worktree (`cf-herdr` "Naming": the intended worktree `cwd` identifies the seat; `.codeflow/rules/worktrees.md`: work happens in `.worktrees/<slug>`), so a subject that follows the method gets `peer_launch_refused` and its trial is invalid. Evidence: TSK-1032 trial round 7 (`.worktrees/tsk-1032/target/qualification/typed-code-r7/builder-adds-type-checker-and-config-model-7/peers.json`): the Codex start requested for `<repository>/.worktrees/tsk-031` was refused with that message, and `observation.json` carries `peer_launch_refused`; round 5 shows the same for `.worktrees/tsk-032`. Both trials ran under the default `--codex-hook-trust=review` option (`launch.json`, `hook_trust.option`). The sibling tasks TSK-1030, TSK-1031 and TSK-1033 open peers the same way when their subjects follow the method; only TSK-1032's refusal is demonstrated here.

Two more checks are keyed to the root path. `trust_choice` (runner.py:306-357) accepts a folder-trust dialog only when it names the fixture path, and `observe_peer` passes `Path(run["repository"])` to `handle_startup` (runner.py:1529). Codex keys hook trust by the absolute path of `.codex/hooks.json` (`evals/qualification/README.md:101`), so a Codex peer in a worktree shows "Hooks need review" even after the operator's pre-launch review of the fixture root, and the runner refuses that screen (runner.py:308-311). The worktree does not exist before launch, so `print-hook-review` (runner.py:1114) cannot cover it.

The subject runs as the operator's user and can write every file the runner reads, git's worktree metadata included. The checks below are therefore bounded evidence, not proof of ownership: each one is a concrete predicate the runner evaluates at a stated moment, and the record names what polling cannot see.

context.heading: Admission: the directory and its repository identity

context: A peer's working directory `C` is accepted when it is the fixture repository root, as today, or passes every check below, all evaluated on the raw path first and on realpaths second, with `lstat` so that a symlink is seen rather than followed:

items.text: Fixture identity, captured once at `launch` into `launch.json` (`peers.fixture_identity`): the realpath of the repository `R` and the realpath of its common directory from `git -C R rev-parse --git-common-dir`, which must be `R/.git`, a real directory.
Placement: `C` is lexically `R/.worktrees/<name>`, one level down; `R`, `R/.worktrees` and `C` are real directories, none a symlink; `os.path.realpath(C) == C`.

Link file: `C/.git` is a regular file under a small size cap holding exactly one line `gitdir: <A>`; `A`, resolved against `C` when relative, is a real directory lexically `R/.git/worktrees/<id>`, one level down, with `R/.git`, `R/.git/worktrees` and `A` real directories and no symlink among them; `os.path.realpath(A) == A`.

Reciprocal pair: `A/gitdir` is a regular file whose content, resolved and realpath'd, is exactly `C/.git`; `A/commondir` is a regular file whose content, resolved against `A` and realpath'd, is exactly the fixture's common directory from step 1. A changed `commondir`, a backlink to another worktree, a symlink or any non-regular file in this chain refuses.

Git's own view, read in a clean subprocess environment (every `GIT_*` variable unset, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null`, `GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1`, `HOME` set to an empty temporary directory): `git -C R worktree list --porcelain` lists a non-main `worktree` entry whose realpath is `C`, neither `bare` nor `prunable`; `git -C C rev-parse --git-common-dir` realpath'd equals the fixture's common directory; `git -C C rev-parse --show-toplevel` realpath'd equals `C`. A git error, a missing, ambiguous or prunable entry refuses.

The accepted identity is pinned to the launch at bind: `C`, `A`, the common directory and the SHA-256 of the contents of `C/.git`, `A/gitdir` and `A/commondir`. A later check that yields a different identity, including a re-registered `A`, is a failure, never a new acceptance.

context: Names are never matched. Other worktree locations (`.claude/worktrees`, harness homes) and nested directories stay refused.

The identity checks, and under `--codex-hook-trust=bypass` the hook content checks against `C/.codex` (`codex_hook_preflight` on the worktree: `hooks.json` equal to the shipped contract-3 definitions, no other hook source, no symlink; the evaluator-home checks as today; `hooks_sha256` is the hash of the file the peer's Codex reads), run at every one of these moments:

items.text: when a request is answered (`peer_decision`);
at bind (`verify_peer_process` from `observe_peer`);
inside `before_key`, immediately before every startup key (`accept_workspace_trust`, `decline_renderer`), in addition to the process identity recheck it makes today;
at readiness, before the ready record is written;
on every later poll of a launch whose status is `ready`: `observe_peer` no longer returns before verification for a ready launch (runner.py:1514).

context: A failure at any moment revokes the ready record (`set_gate(run, pane, None)`), sets the launch to `unverified` with the failing predicate in `error`, and the trial carries `peer_launch_unverified`; no key is sent and nothing restores the launch. `identity_of` (runner.py:1419) stays the process identity; the pinned worktree identity is checked beside it, not folded into it, so a registration-only change with pid, argv, cwd and environment unchanged is still caught.

Limitation, stated in the README: the watcher polls, and a gap longer than `WATCH_GAP_SECONDS` between two completed polls invalidates coverage (`peer_watch_incomplete`, read back by `watch_gaps`); the watcher does not guarantee a poll within that interval, cannot see a change removed and restored between two polls, and no check-then-use step is atomic against an unrestricted same-user writer. This is the runner's existing posture for root peers; the new paths add no stronger claim.

context.heading: Exact-path trust and the folder-trust finish allowance

context: The accepted directory becomes that launch's subject path. `handle_startup` and `trust_choice` receive the launch's verified cwd instead of the fixture root, so a folder-trust dialog (Claude "Accessing workspace:", Codex "Folder access", Grok "Do you trust the contents of this directory?") must name exactly that path; a dialog naming the root for a worktree peer, or a worktree for a root peer, refuses with no key, as any other path does today.

The folder-trust change `finish` allows (`config_drift`, runner.py:1075-1089; `codex_trust_entry`, runner.py:1026-1038) extends to a `trust_level = "trusted"` project entry for an accepted worktree path after a recorded folder-trust acceptance for exactly that path. Each recorded acceptance allows at most its own entry, with no other key in it; two accepted worktrees, or the root and a worktree, are each matched to their own acceptance; the rest of the file keeps its baseline (the whole `projects` table is not stripped); any other folder-trust change stays `evaluator_config_drift`. This rule covers folder trust only; no hook-trust change is allowed at finish.
The decision and launch records carry the accepted path, its kind (`repository` or `worktree`) and the pinned identity, and the refusal text names both accepted forms.

context.heading: Hook review in a worktree created during the trial: decided, route B

context: Under the default `review` option a Codex peer in a worktree meets "Hooks need review" because Codex keys hook trust by the absolute path of `hooks.json`; the worktree does not exist before launch, so the pre-launch review cannot cover it; and the runner never answers that screen or waits for an answer it cannot attribute to a human (runner.py:308-311). The admission work above does not change that, so under `review` a worktree Codex peer moves from `peer_launch_refused` to `peer_startup_refused` and the trial stays invalid.

Operator decision, 2026-10-31 12:52, saved on the status page and relayed by the coordinator: route B. TSK-1032's trials run with the runner's existing per-trial `--codex-hook-trust=bypass`, the choice the README already assigns to the person running the evaluation (`evals/qualification/README.md:105`). Under it the runner's hook content check runs against the worktree's own `hooks.json` at every moment listed above, and under `review` a worktree Codex peer stays refused at its hook screen with no key. The runner's never-answer-hook-screens contract is unchanged, and the finish allowance stays folder trust only. TSK-1032's prerequisite: its AC-4 native trials are launched with `--codex-hook-trust=bypass` once this task lands.

Not chosen, recorded for later tracking if wanted: route A, an operator-authorized, digest-bound review of the shipped hooks for a worktree created mid-trial, which would change the never-answer contract and would first need Codex's supported native trust mechanism investigated. No record owns it; it can be filed as its own task if the default option is ever required for worktree peers.

Alternatives rejected on evidence: pre-creating the review worktree at launch changes a trial that asks the subject to create its own worktree, so its fidelity, although a pre-created path could be verified structurally; waiting at "Hooks need review" in the peer pane cannot tell the operator from the subject typing through the real Herdr binary, and the hook-trust record Codex would write is config drift.

Non-goals: Herdr's own `worktree create|open` stays refused in `peer_shim.py`; the subject seat's checks, the peer flag allowlist, the plugin checks and every other refusal are unchanged; the runner never answers a hook screen; no hook-review bypass is added beyond the existing per-trial option.

TSK-1103.title: A project check runs from the trusted base before any candidate code
TSK-1103.about: After this merges, an adopter can declare a project check that the managed CI runs from the trusted base before any candidate code, and a pull request cannot skip, replace or weaken it.

next.reason: task TSK-1103 depends on TSK-336, whose anchored status is 'todo', not complete

context: Issue #437 (2026-10-30): the managed `codeflow-ci.yml` runs the gate from the pull request's merge checkout, so a project check that decides how the candidate is judged runs the candidate's own copy, and the candidate can skip, replace or widen it. Confirmed on the line at `0ce66e072`: the gates job checks out the merge ref (`assets/base/ci/codeflow-ci.yml:52-54`), picks `essential` or `full` from the head's `.codeflow/test-config.json` (`:176`), sources the head's `.codeflow/ci-setup.sh` (`:189-191`) and runs `codeflow test` on the head's config (`:196`); the setup hook is documented as not a security boundary (`assets/base/ci/README.md:273-282`) and `codeflow ci` only notes a change to it (`ci.rs:2124-2153`). The only base-read input today is the pin (`codeflow-ci.yml:58`, `:70`). `codeflow-policy.yml` checks out the base SHA (`:71`), fetches the head as data (`:183-193`) and runs the fixed `codeflow ci` (`:229`), with no project slot. Existing work covers the pieces, not the slot: TSK-1020 (complete) added `codeflow test --config`; TSK-1001 AC-18 takes this repository's own gate from the base config; TSK-336 makes the default branch the only authority for the hosted verdict jobs and refuses a head that changes `codeflow-ci.yml` (AC-14); TSK-1077 is local hook policy; TSK-294 reads one project hook from the trusted commit for the dependency audit only.

This task adds the general slot: a project-owned declaration of checks that the managed CI runs from the trusted commit's copies before any candidate code, with the base, head and merge commits and the head repository as arguments, failing the required check on the script's exit status. The declaration lives in a project-owned file `codeflow update` never writes. The home is the trusted verdict job of TSK-336 (`pull_request_target`, default-branch files, the head as git data only), because a `pull_request` workflow runs the head's own copy and could drop the step. Non-goal: a project check that needs candidate code or a toolchain stays in the gates job and outside this task; `codeflow test` is unchanged.

TSK-1104.title: Read-only git stays allowed while the policy authority is unresolved
TSK-1104.about: After this merges, an agent whose policy authority cannot be resolved can still read the repository state with git and sees a refusal that names the refs involved and the step that clears it, while every mutating command stays refused.
context: Issue #440 (2026-10-31) reports the state the coordinator found on 2026-10-30 (queue item 27): while a planning amendment on a line retargets a task record and `main` still holds the old target, `landed_policy::declared_target` refuses every hook call on that task's branch, `git status` included, with "landed task records disagree on the policy target". TSK-1077 (PR 441 at `1ddbac7cc`) removes the cause: `landed_policy.rs` no longer reads task records, `declared_target` and the records-disagree refusal are gone (`crates/codeflow-cli/tests/policy_authority.rs:167`), and the `ends_with("/<target>")` match the issue's last point names is gone from `landed_policy.rs` (`cmd/ci/context.rs:384` keeps a `declared_target` for range bounding, without `ends_with`). Verified by the TSK-1077 builder on 2026-10-31 07:50 and read again when this task was planned.

What stays open, and is this task: every guarded command still refuses when the authority cannot be resolved at all (`hook.rs:260-268`, `479-487`, `530-535`; `git_guard.rs` `check_authority`), `git status` and `git rev-parse` included, while the guard already allows read-only git when a target is unresolved (`git_guard.rs:6767-6776`, test at `10974-10997`). The issue asks for read-only git while authority is in doubt, a journey test for the amendment-in-flight state, and the refusal to name the refs and the clearing step. Allowing anything while the authority is unknown is a security decision, so this task records it with the exact command set and why none of those commands can change refs, configuration, hooks or the working tree. Non-goals: no mutating command is allowed without a resolved authority; the policy source rules of TSK-1077 and TSK-1057 are unchanged.

TSK-1105.title: A builder creates its task worktree and claims under its harness sandbox
TSK-1105.about: After this merges, a Claude or Codex builder can create its task worktree, claim, reserve and push from inside its harness sandbox with no unsandboxed retry and every enforcement-path deny still in force.
context: Two harness sandboxes stop a builder before its first commit. Codex builder seats (the `cf-builder` posture) cannot finish a build here: the Codex sandbox denies the `.git/config` write `git worktree add` makes, denies `ps`, which `coordination/scripts/gate-turn.sh` uses to prove a ticket holder is alive, and denies the gate lock holder record under `~/.codeflow/locks/` (`full-gate.lock: Operation not permitted`), so a Codex builder cannot claim, run `codeflow reserve` or push (queue items 29 and 29b, 2026-10-31; TSK-1077, TSK-323 and TSK-330 were reassigned to Claude builders for this reason). In a scaffolded project, Claude's sandbox write-deny on `.claude/` (an enforcement path) makes the required `git worktree add` fail on `.claude/agents/*.md`, so a subject cannot start a task worktree without the auto-mode unsandboxed retry; in the TSK-1032 trials one subject stopped to ask the user and the other retried with the sandbox off (queue item 30, 2026-10-31 01:15). Every Claude builder and every adopter on the sandboxed preset meets this.

This task gives both a sanctioned route that works inside the sandbox without weakening any deny: `codeflow work claim` (one step with the claim commit and preflight, operator decision D4 of 2026-11-01) creates the worktree through a route the presets allow, with the enforcement-path denies judged on the worktree's own copies after checkout as TSK-399 requires; the Codex builder posture gets a lock home its profile allows and a liveness proof that does not need `ps`. Non-goals: no deny is relaxed, no preset gains a broad allow, and the coordination scripts are the workspace's (`coordination/` is not in this repository); this task changes the shipped posture and the `codeflow` commands they call.

TSK-1106.title: The shipped presets deny secret-bearing files by kind and keep source readable
TSK-1106.about: After this merges, an agent under the shipped presets can read a source file whose name contains secret or credentials, and still cannot read a secret-bearing file such as `.env`, a key or a credentials JSON.
context: The shipped Claude presets (`assets/base/settings/default.json`, `acceptEdits.json`, `bypass-sandboxed.json`, mirrored in `crates/codeflow-core/src/security/actions.json`) deny `Read(**/*secret*)` and `Read(**/*credentials*)` and try to exempt source code with negated entries such as `Read(!**/*secret*.rs)`. On 2026-10-31 the TSK-397 builder found that the Read tool still denied `crates/codeflow-cli/tests/refusal_journey/secret_paths.rs`: the negated entries do not take effect as permission rules, while the sandbox read list does honour them (queue item 34). An adopter whose source names contain `secret` or `credentials` (a secrets module, a credentials parser, their tests) cannot read those files through the editor tools; two TSK-397 test edits waited on the operator for this reason. The fix replaces the broad name deny with patterns that name secret-bearing file kinds, after the Claude Code permission-rule semantics are verified against the current documentation and a live probe. Non-goal: the sandbox read list and the hooks' secret-path rules (TSK-335, TSK-1002) are unchanged; only the editor permission rules change, and no deny that covers a real secret file is dropped.

TSK-1107.title: codeflow ci notes a change to the project audit exception check
TSK-1107.about: After this merges, a reviewer sees a `codeflow ci` note whenever a pull request edits the project's dependency-audit exception check, as they already do for the CI setup hook.
context: `codeflow ci` prints a note when a range edits `.codeflow/ci-setup.sh` (`ci.rs:2124-2153`) because the managed CI sources that file. TSK-294 (PR 446) adds a second project-owned file the managed CI reads, the dependency audit exception check, and the Codex review of that PR found that `codeflow ci` does not note a change to it (queue item 37, 2026-10-31 11:54). Codex judged it non-material, since the check cannot change its own pull request's verdict (it is read from the trusted commit), and the coordinator tracked it as a small task. The fix gives the audit exception check the same note with its own engine remedy code, and the sibling sweep covers every project-owned file the managed CI reads so the next one (TSK-1103's declared checks) gets the note in its own task. Non-goal: no verdict changes.

TSK-1108.title: Seat trust prompts follow a recorded hook-trust rule, else the operator
TSK-1108.about: After this merges, an agent running a Herdr seat in any project knows from the shipped instructions that a hook-trust prompt goes to the operator unless that project records an operator-authorized hook-trust rule, how it verifies the rule is landed, current and unrevoked, what the rule lets it approve and how it checks the hooks, and what it must refuse; in this repository the recorded rule lets it answer the prompt itself.
context: On 2026-10-30 at 20:00 the operator gave a standing rule directly in the coordinator's session (queue item 28): in this repository, agents answer Herdr seat hook-trust and folder-trust prompts themselves after reading each prompt in full, and approve once only CodeFlow's own hooks that match `origin/main`, never trust-all unread and never always-approve. On 2026-10-31 at about 17:15 EDT the operator confirmed it directly in the coordinator's session: "yes, agents should be able to answer the herdr prompts on the sessions that they manage including folder trust and hook trust prompts - or else we can't have autonomy - the key is to have things protected in other ways including sandbox and the guards and other protections." The scope is the Herdr seats the agents manage in this repository's worktrees, folder trust and hook trust. That rule is this repository's recorded hook-trust rule, and its home is one line in the project section of this repository's `AGENTS.md` (the AGENTS.md row "receive a standing operator rule"; `cf-method/references/autonomy.md` "Recorded rules and delegations"; no config key holds seat prompts).

It is not a default for adopters. The shipped texts say hook trust is the operator's: `cf-herdr/SKILL.md:128` and `:181`, `transport.md` "First-run prompts" (ADR-0075, amendment of 2026-10-03), and `autonomy.md` "Trust prompts" (near `:133`) and its hook example (near `:230`), which say an agent never answers a hook-trust prompt. An adopter whose operator gave no such rule keeps that route. This task makes the shipped rule conditional: a hook-trust prompt goes to the operator unless the consuming project's own `AGENTS.md` project section records an operator-authorized hook-trust rule that meets the landed-record checks of "Recorded rules and delegations" (present on the protected target branch as fetched from the canonical repository, landed by a pull request a person merged, citing the operator's approval as the forge attributes it, with the actions, the trusted ref and the revocation event named). Under such a rule the agent approves once, after reading the whole prompt, only when every hook file the prompt names is byte-identical to the trusted ref's copy, and refuses and reports everything else. The folder-trust text matches the workspace rule of 2026-09-22 already in `autonomy.md` "Trust prompts".

The same shipped section today rules this out: `autonomy.md:160` says a delegation names a human delegate, and `:205-209` say delegation never transfers hook trust and a person performs it, and ADR-0075 (its 2026-10-03 amendment, and "Hook trust is the operator's" near `:327`) says agents never review or trust hook definitions. This task therefore reconciles that section and the ADR explicitly rather than adding a sentence that competes with them: the hook-trust rule is a narrow standing rule the operator authorizes for one project, not a delegation to a human delegate; the human-delegate rule stays for every other delegated decision; the hard gates stay (canonical repository, protected target, an independently attributable human merge, the operator's approval evidence; a timestamp, a chat message or a peer's claim never satisfies them); credentials, protected branches and irreversible actions stay a person's. Before every answer the seat checks the grant is current and unrevoked: fetch the protected target from the canonical repository, confirm the line is present at the fetched tip and its landing pull request and approval still verify, and confirm no later landed change or ADR-0075 amendment withdrew it; a grant that is missing, unreadable, unlanded, unverifiable or revoked keeps the operator route.

TSK-1120.title: cf-present documents open in a dashboard shell with a side menu, tabs and drill-down views

context: The operator's feedback of 2026-10-31 on the hand-built 4.0.0 status page: a report page needs proper structure for how it reports different aspects, changed by choosing a tab or the like; a proper side menu, like a proper dashboard, with drill-downs; even tasks need proper context sometimes; and this belongs in `cf-present`, not only for reports, neither rigid nor random, so that each page is not a fresh design with no consistency. Figure: the shell's regions; the side menu is the view tree, the breadcrumb is the path down it, the context strip is the current view's facts, and tabs switch aspects inside the view.
Decisions, each reversible and disclosed here:

items.text: **The shell is declared, not drawn by the author.** The document gains an optional `views` array beside `blocks`; a view has `id`, `title`, `kind`, optional `context` (one to eight labelled facts, each `label`, `text` and an optional `state` or location mark from the grammar vocabulary), `blocks` (the existing catalog; `tabs` and `disclosure` included) and `children` (nested views). The root `blocks` of a document with `views` are the header's anchor (the first narrative and the orienting figure, as the bar of TSK-1097 requires) and render above every view. A `reference` of kind `view` (`document.rs:514`, the existing frame-reference shape) in any block opens that view; the runtime draws the breadcrumb from the tree, never from the author. The side menu lists the tree to the depth the document declares, with the current view marked and the view's `summary` mark or count when it carries one (TSK-1096 AC-9's summary vocabulary); at phone width it is a drawer behind one button. The sections rail of today lists the current view's sections inside the body.

**Outcomes first is the contract's primary structure.** The operator's direction of 2026-10-31 (13:15): a report is organised by outcomes first, and every outcome opens to its detail. The contract therefore fixes the root view as an `overview` whose body lists the document's outcomes (each with its state, percent and next step where the kind has them), each outcome a `view` reference into its own `topic` view, and the tree under a topic going to `item` views and their `evidence`; the side menu's first group is those outcomes, and other kinds (`list`, `timeline`, `issues`, `decisions`, `evidence`, `commands`) are cross-cutting entries after it. This is the shape every registry document has, not an option an author picks.

**View kinds are a registry, with room.** `kind` is one of `overview` (the first view, the outcomes and the decision picture), `topic` (a group of items with a percent, what it is, done and not done, and its reasoning), `item` (one thing with its context strip), `list` (an encoded table of items), `timeline` (a schedule figure and its windows), `issues` (blocked and owed items), `decisions` (operator inputs as `decision` and `form` blocks), `evidence` (coverage and refs), `commands` (one runnable script) or `custom` with a one-line `reason`. The registry fixes what a reader finds in each kind (the layout contract below) and `present check` warns on a `custom` view, naming the registry, so a new kind that recurs is added to the registry with a specimen once, and never improvised. Adding a kind is a change to this registry and its specimen, not to the shell.

**The layout contract.** One reference section in `document-authoring.md` names the regions (side menu, header, breadcrumb, context strip, tabs, body, drawer), the order a view's body follows (lead line, the answering figure or encoded table, short acting text, then disclosures), the component set that fills a body (the catalog blocks, the figure families, the encoded table, the `schedule` family, the `decision` and `form` blocks, labelled `code`), and what each registry kind must carry; the specimen page renders every kind once. A document that follows the contract looks like every other document that does, and the contract leaves content free; it is the consistency the operator asked for and the `custom` kind is the flexibility.

**Drill-down is navigation, not duplication.** A child view is declared once and reached from any `reference`; the same task view serves the release, the epic and the theme that link to it. The breadcrumb is the declared path to the current view; a reference from elsewhere keeps the tree's path, so a reader always knows where a view lives.

**Export and comments.** The export renders the shell with the side menu as a static outline, every view present in tree order with its breadcrumb as a heading path, and the first view shown when scripts are off, so a capture holds everything. Comment anchors bind to blocks inside views as they bind today; a view id is part of the anchor's context so a moved block in another view is not re-anchored by mistake.

**Capacity holds the largest report it must carry (Codex round 8, F1).** A status document for a scope of 300 tasks declares one `item` view per task (TSK-1098 AC-10), so a document-wide cap of a few dozen views or 512 blocks (`limits.rs:5`, `MAX_BLOCKS`; `:11`, `MAX_FIGURE_BLOCKS` 24) cannot hold it. The budgets are therefore scoped: the existing block, nesting and figure budgets of `limits.rs` apply per view (each view is one block tree of at most 512 blocks and 24 figures, as a linear document is today), and the document gains a view budget of 1024 views, a view depth of four and a total of 16384 blocks and the existing 8 MiB document size, each refused by name; the runtime renders the current view into the page and keeps the other views as parsed data, so a large document stays responsive, and the export writes every view. Every task stays reachable through the outcomes path; the generator never drops a drill-down to fit, and a document over the budget is refused, never truncated.

**The stored revision is bounded with the document (Codex round 9, F6).** The store pretty-serialises each revision (`state.rs:4196`), `update` publishes a revision and moves the current-session pointer without checking that revision's own read limit (`state.rs:1250`, `:1259`), and every later read enforces `MAX_REVISION_STATE_BYTES`, the document budget plus 1 MiB (`limits.rs:63`, `state.rs:4020`). A 16001-block document of short narratives fits 8 MiB compact and exceeds that read limit once pretty-printed, so it would open, store and then never read, show or export again. This task owns the reconciliation: before `open` or `update` writes anything, the store serialises the revision envelope exactly as it will persist it (`RevisionContent`, context and snapshots included) and refuses by name when that representation would exceed the read limit, before any session state changes, so the current revision never advances to one that cannot be read back; the resource bound stays, and the accepted document budget is whichever is smaller of the declared block and byte budgets and the representation bound. The builder decides in AC-1 whether to keep pretty serialisation with the read limit raised to hold the declared budget plus its formatting overhead, or to store compact JSON under the present limit, and records the choice; either way the pre-write check is what admits a revision. A `custom` view, `title`, `label`, `text` and `reason` are text through the existing sanitiser; `html` stages inside a view keep their frame and sandbox (ADR-0049).

**Check ownership (Codex round 8, F4).** This task owns the `present check` warning for an `html` stage in a view whose registry kind names a catalog carrier for its content (a `timeline` view with a stage instead of the `schedule` family, a `list` view with a stage instead of an encoded table); TSK-1121 owns the missing-`topic` warning; TSK-1097 carries the guidance for both and neither check.
